The versions share a core but need not contain identical text. Content negotiation lets a visitor ask for a format at the page's usual URL. Some agents send the request header Accept: text/markdown . A host that supports negotiation responds with Shoalrun's Markdown version. A browser asking for HTML gets the HTML version. The URL stays the same: Request to /publish/output/ Response Browser sends Accept: text/html HTML page, Content-Type: text/html Agent sends Accept: text/markdown Markdown page, Content-Type: text/markdown Accept says what the visitor can use. documents.title: Content and stable IDs
documents.summary: Give each page a durable identity and publish explicit variants.
documents.text: Author pages as .md or .mdx under the content directory, site.contentDir (default content , relative to docs.config.yaml ). The build parses and validates every .md and .mdx file there, drafts included, so a stray README without frontmatter fails the build. The id identifies a document independently of its filename, title, slug, and navigation position. A page's slug sets its public route. The compiler rejects route collisions and duplicate IDs within a publication variant. Keeping identity separate from location lets the documentation grow without reconnecting every reference. A filename is an authoring choice; a slug is a reader's address; the ID is the lasting connection used by links, navigation, and relationships. Renaming a page can leave its ID intact even when its URL needs a redirect. --- id : guide.example title : Example guide summary : A short description for navigation and discovery. type : guide slug : /guides/example channel : production version : current access : { policy : public } --- Publication channel, API version, and language are separate axes. Published pages need channel and version, supplied on the page or through global frontmatter . Language uses global frontmatter defaults/enforced values first, then publications.defaults.language , then en . An explicit page language overrides that default. Enabled publication entries can also omit language to inherit the same default; the project config declares supported combinations and route prefixes. Nonpublic pages are excluded before rendering. The prototype does not yet provide hosted role-based access control. Link to another document by ID with [the guide](doc:guide.example) or <DocLink doc="guide.example">the guide</DocLink> . These become the current route in HTML and the corresponding .md route in Markdown. A slug or filename change leaves ID-based links intact. Unknown IDs fail the build. The current MDX semantic adapters cover GitHub Flavored Markdown and the elements in the component reference , including diagrams . Dynamic expressions and unknown components fail because they cannot yet be represented faithfully in both HTML and Markdown. See published outputs for what an agent receives. Set the root language once, for example: publications : defaults : { channel : production , version : current , language : fr } channels : production : { pathPrefix : "" } versions : current : { pathPrefix : "" } enabled : - { channel : production , version : current } - { channel : production , version : current , language : de } Pages without language use French at their ordinary route. A page with language: de uses the German publication and a /de route prefix. Related reading Read first How Shoalrun works — See how IDs, slugs, and routes fit into the build. Next steps Page metadata — Add the metadata fields each page needs after inheritance. Organize site navigation — Place the page in the site menu. Related topics DocLink — Link to pages by stable ID so links survive slug changes.

documents.title: Let readers choose recipes with a cookbook
documents.summary: Create a page that helps readers choose among complete published recipes.

headings.title: 3. Put the chooser on a cookbook page
Choose single or multiple selection deliberately

documents.text: A cookbook combines an authored introduction with a list or chooser of published recipe pages . It does not read ingredient files. Ingredients have already been copied into the recipes during authoring. This guide uses the Site workflows cookbook . It offers a build check or a build-and-audit check. The audit recipe already includes the build, so the reader chooses one complete path. 1. Prepare the destination recipes Publish each destination as a type: recipe page in the same channel, version, and language as the cookbook. Each recipe should contain the setup, steps, and success checks needed to follow it on its own. Our two destinations are recipe.build-docs and recipe.audit-docs . They can be opened directly, even if the cookbook is removed. See compose and maintain recipes for how their ingredient source becomes a complete page. 2. Configure the choices The following configuration points to those finished pages by stable document ID: docs/config/cookbooks.yaml site-checks : title : How much validation do you need? mode : single options : - id : build label : Build and check page artifacts doc : recipe.build-docs when : You want to confirm an edit produces HTML and Markdown. needs : A Shoalrun checkout and the page's stable ID. outcome : A successful build and checked page files. - id : audit label : Build and run project audits doc : recipe.audit-docs when : You also need the configured API and project checks. needs : A Shoalrun checkout and the page's stable ID. outcome : Checked page files and no failed configured audits. doc selects the recipe. label names the choice. The optional when , needs , and outcome fields explain the choice; they are descriptive text, not requirements the browser verifies. When when is omitted, the recipe's summary is shown. Load this mapping from the project configuration. Shoalrun already has this include: docs/docs.config.yaml cookbooks : { $include : ./config/cookbooks.yaml } 3. Put the chooser on a cookbook page Write an MDX page with type: cookbook , the usual page identity and publication fields, and an introduction explaining the choices. Its body can contain: Choose the level of validation you need. The audit path includes the build. < CookbookChooser id = "site-checks" /> The component's id is the configuration key site-checks . It is separate from the cookbook page's document ID, cookbook.site-workflows . A normal site build publishes the cookbook's own text and chooser. When a reader makes a selection, the browser fetches the selected recipe's HTML and shows the instructions under Your path . It does not call the recipe assembler, fetch ingredients, or execute commands. For a simple directory of recipes, use DocCards instead of a chooser. A page with type: cookbook does not require an interactive component. Choose single or multiple selection deliberately Choose the selection mode based on whether readers should follow one path or combine several. Setting Reader behavior Appropriate use mode: single Choose one recipe with radio buttons. Alternative tasks or overlapping paths, such as build versus build-and-audit. mode: multiple Select several recipes with checkboxes; display them in configuration order. Recipes that the author has checked make sense together. This is the default. Multiple selection displays whole recipe bodies, including any repeated setup. It does not deduplicate steps, connect outputs between recipes, or check their combined dependencies. If a combined task needs shared setup and explicit handoffs, compose it as one recipe and offer that recipe as a choice. What readers and agents receive The published surfaces expose cookbook choices in different forms. Surface Content Cookbook HTML before selection The authored introduction, choices, descriptions, and recipe links. Cookbook HTML after selection The selected published recipe instructions, loaded in the browser. Cookbook Markdown The authored introduction and all choice descriptions and recipe links. Recipe Markdown The complete published instructions for that one recipe. Download Markdown A file containing the selected recipes' instructions. Link to this path preserves the selection in the browser URL. It does not create a new published Markdown page. An agent reading the cookbook's Markdown can choose a recipe link. Give a task-performing agent the recipe's Markdown or the downloaded selection. Print this path prints the loaded instructions. If a recipe cannot load, its source link remains available. Markdown downloads fail as a whole rather than saving an incomplete selection. Without JavaScript, the visible recipe links still work. Check the result Build the site and open the cookbook in HTML and Markdown. For single selection, try each option. For multiple selection, also try the combinations you intend readers to use. Follow each offered workflow and inspect its success checks. The build rejects missing, draft, wrong-type, or wrong-publication recipe targets and duplicate option IDs,

documents.title: Create a note
documents.summary: Preview an API operation page built from a small, fictional OpenAPI file.
documents.text: Fictional API example. This page demonstrates documentation features; its operations do not describe a live service. This page is a live example of an API reference generated by Shoalrun. The source OpenAPI file defines one fictional operation; this introduction is authored in MDX. The build combines them into the operation details below and the example panel on the right. Example only: The Notes API is fictional. These requests are examples, not calls to a live service. OpenAPI for this operation: Download JSON . POST /notes Create a note Save a short note in this fictional API. Servers https://api.example.test Request body Required. application/json object 1 property text string required ⓘ maxLength: 280 The note to save. documents.title: CSS and theme reference
documents.summary: Customize colors, typography, layout, navigation, code, and component styles with one project stylesheet.
documents.text: The built site loads /assets/site.css , which imports /assets/tokens.css . To customize a project, set site.customCss to a local stylesheet. The build copies it to /assets/project.css and links it after the framework CSS on every HTML page. Paths resolve from the config file that declares them, including imported config fragments. The stylesheet is a build dependency, so changes are picked up on rebuild. docs.config.yaml site : title : Example documentation customCss : ./styles/project.css styles/project.css :root { --font-body : Inter , ui-sans-serif , system-ui , sans-serif ; --color-accent : #2458a6 ; --color-link : #2458a6 ; --width-site : 92 rem ; } .page-head h1 { letter-spacing : -.02 em ; } Pages link these stylesheets in order, and later files win: /assets/site.css (which imports tokens.css and header.css ), a preset's /assets/theme.css , the generated /assets/palette.css , the generated /assets/fonts.css , then /assets/project.css . Themes lists when each one is present. To use your own font files, set theme.fonts instead of writing @font-face rules here. The build then copies the files, preloads the body font, and sets --font-body , --font-heading , and --font-code for you. Use tokens for broad changes and the generated classes below for a particular region. The project stylesheet is copied as one file; relative images or @import files are not copied automatically. Use site-root URLs for separately hosted assets. Markdown twins contain content, not CSS. Before writing CSS, check whether a theme preset , palette , or color mode already covers the change. Project CSS loads after all three, so the tokens below override them. The build checks palette colors for contrast. It does not check colors set here. Inline badges use --color-field-surface , --color-ink , and --color-border for neutral ; info , success , warning , and new use the matching callout note, tip, warning, and important tokens. Register a color in badges.variants to add or override a variant with checked light and dark text contrast. The generated /assets/badges.css loads after palette CSS and before project CSS. Typography, shape, and width tokens Use these tokens to adjust text, corner shapes, and content widths. Token Controls --font-body Body and interface font stack. --font-code Inline code, blocks, and small technical labels. --font-heading Page titles and section headings. Defaults to --font-body . --radius-small Inputs, small panels, code, tabs, and disclosures. --radius-panel Larger cards and example panels. --shadow-edge A faint outline and top highlight on code blocks and reef panels. Empty in light mode; palettes set it in dark mode. --width-site Maximum width of the page shell, whether or not a right rail is present. --width-reference Maximum width of the masthead. --landing-width Maximum width of a landing page, a splash section, and their masthead. Defaults to 76rem . --nav-item-height , --nav-item-pad-y Height and vertical padding of navigation rows. Rows are 44px tall for touch and 32px tall with a mouse or trackpad on wider screens. Each preset's font stack starts with its bundled font, followed by a matching fallback face named after it, such as "Inter Fallback" . The fallback is a local system font resized to the bundled font's metrics, so text keeps its place while the font loads. fonts.css defines these faces; with theme.fonts: system , the build omits them and the stacks fall through to system fonts. The root text size is 16px and line height is 1.65 in site.css . Override :root in the project stylesheet if the whole site needs different type scale. Article paragraphs, headings, and code blocks also have local sizes that can be overridden by their selectors. Core color tokens These tokens control the main surface, text, and accent colors. Token Controls --color-text Default body text. --color-page Page background. --color-surface Panels and masthead background. --color-ink Strong headings and controls. --color-link Links at rest. --color-link-hover Hovered links. --color-focus Keyboard focus outline. --color-accent Brand mark and active navigation accent. --color-accent-contrast Text on accent fills, such as a primary header link. Defaults to #fff . --color-strong-surface , --color-strong-text Inked bands and their text, such as the ledger masthead and selected tabs. Default to --color-ink and --color-surface . --color-muted Secondary text and markers. --color-emphasis Eyebrows, markers, and card icons. --color-summary Page summary text. --color-section-heading Smaller headings and tab labels. Borders, fields, and navigation tokens These tokens control boundaries, input fields, and navigation states. Token Controls --color-header-muted Publication label text. --color-header-border Publication label border. --color-border Main outlines and dividers. --color-border-soft Quiet separators within content. --color-border-nested Nested navigation and lists. --color-field-surface Tables, tabs, and input surfaces. --color

documents.title: Data-driven React components
documents.summary: Follow local data through a component plugin, shared documentation, and a React calculator.

headings.title: Use the component in a page
Share the model with the browser

documents.text: Use a declared data file when a component needs to generate tables, calculations, or other structured documentation. This advanced example adds data and generated explanations to the small CopyText example . A data file is optional; ordinary component text can stay in MDX. Where the content lives A custom component is a small program that writes part of a documentation page. Its build function produces shared content, which Shoalrun renders as HTML and Markdown. An optional React interface adds browser controls afterward. Shoalrun does not convert React into Markdown. The retry example splits its work across these files: File What you write there What readers get The page's .mdx file Task-specific explanations and the <RetryBudget /> invocation. The surrounding documentation in HTML and Markdown. policy.json Retry counts, delays, supported status codes, and the safety warning. The configured values and warning in both formats. plugin.mjs Validation, reusable explanatory text, formulas, tables, and code examples. The component's shared HTML and Markdown content. browser.jsx React controls, state, input validation, and the interactive timeline. A browser interface for trying alternative values. style.css Optional styles for the browser interface. The files the HTML page loads for that interface. policy.json is this example's data format, not a Shoalrun requirement. A simpler component can use only MDX attributes and child content. Keep page-specific prose in the page; put recurring explanations and generated content in the plugin. Start with data For example, policy.json contains a complete configured policy: { "attempts" : 4 , "baseDelayMs" : 500 , "maxDelayMs" : 30000 , "backoff" : "exponential" , "jitter" : "none" , "retryableStatuses" : [ 429 , 502 , 503 , 504 ] , "warning" : "Retry only idempotent operations, or requests protected by an idempotency key. Honor a server's Retry-After header; it can require a longer wait than this policy." } The plugin's content() function imports that data, validates it, and returns shared content nodes. This shortened excerpt shows how a value becomes a paragraph; the complete plugin also generates the tables, warning, formula, schedule, code, and link: const policy = validatePolicy (importedPolicy); return { content : c .paragraph ( `Allow at most ${ policy .attempts } attempts, including the first request.` ) , data : policy }; That paragraph becomes <p>Allow at most 4 attempts, including the first request.</p> in HTML and the same sentence in Markdown. There is no separate Markdown renderer to write for these shared nodes. Use the component in a page The page author supplies the surrounding context and invokes the registered component: ## Retrying a request Check whether the operation is safe to repeat before enabling retries. The policy below shows the configured wait budget. < RetryBudget title = "Request retry policy" /> With the example policy, the generated Markdown includes this worked schedule: | Attempt | Wait before attempt | Cumulative wait | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | 0 ms | 0 ms | | 2 | 500 ms | 500 ms | | 3 | 1000 ms | 1500 ms | | 4 | 2000 ms | 3500 ms | HTML displays the same documented schedule. React receives the same validated policy directly and adds the calculator shown below. Changing a browser control changes that reader's calculation; it does not edit policy.json , the documented schedule, or Markdown. To change the documented policy, edit the data file and rebuild. Registration Add registrations to your project configuration: components : - ./components/retry-budget/components.json The manifest declares the build module, browser source, and styles relative to the package. Shoalrun compiles the module graph and includes imported JSON and shared functions in dependency tracking. The build module imports policy.json ; there is no separate files registration. Interactive React example A retry policy is a useful documentation component: readers need to understand the safety rules and calculate how repeated attempts affect total wait time. The packaged examples/components/retry-budget/ folder contains a working plugin, policy data, React source, shared model module, and stylesheet. Copy the whole folder to components/retry-budget/ , then install its dependencies from your project directory: npm ci --prefix components/retry-budget Use the registration above to enable the component. The plugin validates the JSON policy and generates a settings table, formulas, a worked schedule, a warning, a code example, and a specification link. React receives that validated policy as instance data and adds controls for exploring other policies. Both representations start from the same configured values. < RetryBudget title = "Request retry policy" /> Request retry policy Before you retry: Retry only idempotent operations, or requests protected by an idempotency key. Honor a server's Retry-After header; it can require a longer wait than this pol

documents.summary: Register trusted component plugins with shared HTML and Markdown content.
documents.text: A component package adds a custom component, such as <CopyText> , that authors can use in their pages. Its content() function produces the content shown in both HTML and Markdown. An optional browser module adds interactive behavior. Use a component Install the component package and add its exported manifest to your configuration. For a local component, register its manifest path: components : - ./components/copy-text/components.json An installed package can export its manifest as its entry point, or as a subpath such as @acme/docs-components/shoalrun . Replace that illustrative name with your installed package's export. Paths resolve relative to the configuration file that declares them, including includes and presets. The page supplies the content: < CopyText > Contact support@example.com for help. </ CopyText > Contact support@example.com for help. CopyText requires child content and accepts no attributes. Its copy button is optional browser behavior. Markdown retains the authored text: Contact < support@example.com > for help. Develop a component The package's manifest declares its names and implementation files. Consumers register this manifest once; they do not configure its internal browser files: { "apiVersion" : 1 , "components" : { "CopyText" : { "module" : "./plugin.mjs" , "browser" : "./browser.jsx" } } } Each component needs module . browser and a styles list are optional. These paths are relative to the manifest. Names start with an uppercase letter, contain only letters and digits, and must be unique across registrations. They cannot replace built-ins. The complete build module for the small example passes the page's children through unchanged: import { defineComponent } from '@shoalrun/cli/components' ; export default defineComponent ({ children : 'required' , content ({ children }) { return children; } }); A component that generates documentation uses the supported content helpers: import { defineComponent , content as c } from '@shoalrun/cli/components' ; export default defineComponent ({ attributes : { label : { type : 'string' , required : true } } , children : 'required' , content ({ attributes , children }) { return [ c .paragraph ( c .strong ( attributes .label)) , children]; } }); Helpers include paragraph , strong , emphasis , inlineCode , code , heading , link , list , table , group , and component . They create shared content without requiring compiler-node objects. component composes an existing Shoalrun component using its documented attributes. Raw HTML and representation filters are unsupported. content() is required. A missing function or empty result fails with a diagnostic; there is no separate HTML-only renderer. It receives validated attributes and the authored children. It runs once per invocation before either output is rendered. Attributes and children Attribute schemas define the values page authors may supply: Setting Meaning type string , boolean , or number . required Whether the attribute must be present when it has no default. default A value matching the declared type and constraints. values Allowed string values. min , max , integer Optional numeric constraints. Booleans accept a bare attribute or quoted "true" and "false" . Numbers use quoted literals such as attempts="4" . Dynamic expressions are unsupported. Unknown or duplicate attributes fail. The TypeScript API infers attribute types from the schema. children is none by default, or optional or required . Return the supplied children to preserve page-authored content. Use content.component to compose built-ins with more specific child rules. Browser data and behavior For an interactive component, resolve its model in content() and return both shared documentation and browser data: content ({ attributes }) { const policy = makePolicy (attributes); return { content : describePolicy (policy) , data : policy }; } makePolicy and describePolicy represent your component's model and content functions. data must contain only JSON values. Shoalrun snapshots it per invocation and gives that same data to the browser. Do not recover data by parsing tables or matching display labels. Import shared validation and calculation functions into both implementations when they need the same behavior. The browser module exports an enhancement function: export async function enhance ({ root , controls , content , data }) { // Mount optional controls into the empty controls element. // Read the instance model from data, not from presentation markup. // Keep the shared documentation in content intact. // Reveal controls after mounting; return when the interface is ready. } root contains this component instance; content contains its rendered documentation. React can mount into controls . Browser behavior enhances the shared documentation; this is not an arbitrary React renderer or an MDX import mechanism. If enhancement fails or JavaScript is disabled, shared content remains readable. The data-driven React fixtur

documents.title: Metadata customization
documents.summary: Defaults, enforcement, custom field declarations, text selection, and provider contracts.

headings.title: Read metadata from a project module

documents.text: Use this guide when your project needs shared metadata rules or fields beyond the native page metadata . To choose which values appear in published Markdown, see Markdown metadata . Global defaults and enforced values The project config is the root docs.config.yaml plus any imported fragments. Its frontmatter block supplies shared page values; this block does not appear inside an individual page's header. Configure it in the root file or an imported fragment: frontmatter : locales : { en : en-US } defaults : type : guide channel : production version : v1 language : en audiences : [ developers ] access : { policy : draft } seo : description : Documentation for the example API. variables : product : Payments enforced : audiences : [ partners ] editorial : owner : API documentation fields : editorial.owner : type : string description : Team responsible for the documentation. defaults fills in values that a page may replace. enforced sets values the page cannot replace. Precedence is defaults → page frontmatter → enforced values . Objects merge recursively, and arrays replace rather than concatenate. In this example, every page's effective audience is partners , even if its source lists another audience. A page can override the default SEO description, but cannot override the enforced editorial owner. The id and slug fields must stay on each page; they cannot be global defaults or enforced values. Other native and custom metadata can be inherited. Required fields and declared types are checked after merging, so an inherited type , summary , or required custom field satisfies validation. The generated JSON Schema omits inherited fields from its source-level required lists. Global values do not bypass public metadata projection rules. access follows the same precedence. A default public policy allows a page to remain an explicit draft. An enforced public policy replaces even an explicit draft policy, so use defaults if authors need to keep individual pages unpublished. Scaffolded files are still initially written with draft access. For language, a page uses the enforced language, its own language, the frontmatter default, publications.defaults.language , then en , in that order. Enabled publication entries that omit language use the enforced/default global language, then the publication default, then en . The current router leaves the default language unprefixed. Future translation URL conventions remain open. frontmatter.locales sets the usual formatting locale for each language. documents.title: Check a deployed site
documents.summary: Run the provider-neutral HTTP checker after publishing and before release.
documents.text: A local build verifies the generated files. After deployment, check what the host actually serves. From the framework/ directory in a Shoalrun checkout, pass the deployed site origin to the post-deploy checker: npm run deploy:check -- https://docs.example.com/ Use the real HTTPS site URL and a trailing slash, including a configured base path such as https://docs.example.com/docs/ . The command does not change the deployed site. For a branch deployment, pass the full hash that the deployment job checked out. The checker reads /build-info.json and fails if that domain serves a different revision: npm run deploy:check -- https://docs.example.com/ --source-commit "$SOURCE_COMMIT" SOURCE_COMMIT must be a 40- or 64-character Git commit hash. Supply it from the job that deploys this origin, for example git rev-parse HEAD after checkout. A missing or mismatched record is a failure. For a site with hosted chat and search, add --chat . It checks the public chat settings and both endpoints: GET returns 405, a foreign origin returns 403, and an invalid same-origin request returns 400. Invalid requests stop before model or embedding calls. If chat is already paused, use --chat --chat-paused instead; the checker expects its 503 paused response. It does not change the pause flag. npm run deploy:check -- https://docs.example.com/ --chat What it checks The checker reads the deployed /documents.json and tests every listed page: HTML at the page URL with Accept: text/html , including its content type, Vary: Accept , and alternate Markdown Link header. Markdown at the same URL with Accept: text/markdown , including its content type, Vary , Content-Location , and alternate link. The direct .md URL and exact text equality between its body and the negotiated Markdown body. Each page's og:url and og:image point to the checked public origin. When pages have share images, it fetches one image and checks that the host serves it as an image. Canonical links point to the page being checked, and noindex matches the manifest's indexing choice. /robots.txt advertises the sitemap when one exists. Every sitemap URL matches an indexable manifest page, every indexable page is listed once, and lastmod matches its metadata. The checker fetches child sitemaps and catches redirects and HTTP errors. It also checks /llms.txt , /resource-headers.json , and the API catalog when the resource headers declare one. It verifies discovery content types and that a random missing route returns 404 for both HTML and Markdown requests. This establishes the host's response behavior; it does not judge whether the authored HTML and Markdown prose mean the same thing. Read the result The command prints a PASS or FAIL summary with request, document, and failure counts. On failure, each FAIL line names the route and the missing or incorrect response. For example, a Markdown response served as HTML is reported as a Content-Type failure. Fix the host route or headers, deploy again, and rerun the checker before release. Exit status 0 means every check passed, 1 means the deployed site failed one or more checks, and 2 means the command input is invalid. A passing result does not replace manual review, accessibility checks, or an external scorecard. The content negotiation guide defines the host-independent HTTP contract. The Vercel guide shows one hosting recipe. The checker works against any provider that serves the same contract. Related reading Related topics Host and limit documentation chat — Check a deployed site's headers, redirects, and Markdown negotiation. (Status: experimental.) Often confused with Audit a docs project — The audit checks project sources in CI; the deployment check tests the published site over HTTP.

documents.title: Design templates
documents.summary: Make repeatable page structures that help authors and agents serve readers.
documents.text: A template defines the starting structure of a page. Use it for information that belongs in most pages of a particular kind. A writing guide explains how to write that information. Start with a reader need Choose the page's purpose before choosing headings. A how-to helps a reader complete a task; a reference supports lookup; an explanation builds understanding; a tutorial teaches through a guided exercise. Keep distinct needs on separate pages when combining them makes either harder to use. For an ingredient, define one reusable action, its inputs, and its success check. For a recipe, give the complete ordered procedure and recovery advice. A cookbook helps readers choose among recipes. These structures support reuse without making readers assemble their own instructions. Make prompts actionable A useful placeholder asks for specific missing information: prerequisites, a tested command, expected output, or a recovery action. Avoid vague prompts such as “add useful details.” Tell the agent to flag missing evidence instead of filling gaps with plausible facts. Keep required sections small. Make optional sections clearly optional, and provide a reviewed example outside the template. A copied example's technical details are not evidence for a different feature. Keep structure and checks separate Shoalrun's template overrides control scaffold text. They do not automatically change configured lint rules. Match the template to your page-type conventions and configure checks explicitly. Review a template by drafting several real pages with it. Remove sections authors repeatedly leave empty, and add prompts where readers repeatedly lack information. Check both HTML and Markdown so essential instructions survive every representation. Related reading Reference while working Templates — Configure project template overrides. Design a writing guide — Give agents editorial guidance alongside the page structure.

documents.title: Design a writing guide
documents.summary: Give authors and agents clear editorial rules, examples, and review expectations.
documents.text: A project writing guide explains your readers, terminology, and editorial decisions. Give your agent the guide's file path in project instructions so it can read the same rules as human authors. Put guidance in project configuration Use authoring to give agents shared editorial instructions and file paths: authoring : directives : | Write for the reader's task. Verify technical claims against inspected sources. Use Steps for titled procedures; leave numbers out of headings. guideFiles : - content/writing-guide.mdx exemplarFiles : - content/reviewed-how-to.mdx Paths are relative to docs.config.yaml and point to files your agent should read. docs context returns this guidance and its configuration owner. For a new page, your agent can read it with config resolve . Shoalrun validates the field shapes; it does not load these files into a model, run the instructions, or require a provider key. These authoring settings do not configure a model. State the decisions that matter Describe who reads the docs, what they already know, and what they need to accomplish. Define preferred product names and terms, how to introduce unfamiliar concepts, and how much explanation different page types need. Separate rules from preferences. Give a reason when it changes how a writer should decide. For example: “Use Steps for a titled procedure so readers can scan the sequence; leave numbers out of heading text.” Show reviewed examples Pair a short rule with a concrete example or link to a reviewed page. Explain what makes the example useful. Choose examples for the same reader purpose: an API reference is a poor model for an introductory explanation. Include ingredients, recipes, and cookbooks if your project uses them. Explain what belongs in a reusable action, a complete procedure, and a page that helps readers choose. The example writing guide shows this site's choices. Adapt it to your own readers rather than treating it as a required Shoalrun style. Define evidence and review expectations Tell the agent to support changed technical claims with sources it has inspected, verify examples when possible, and report missing facts. Your agent handles source discovery and evidence gathering with its own tools. Keep editorial examples separate from factual sources. Define what the reviewer needs: a diff, changed claims and their sources, check results, and unresolved questions. Do not treat a clean style report as approval to publish. Automate the repeatable rules Use Vale or your preferred checker for rules it can assess reliably. Put the command and configuration path in project instructions. Keep judgment about clarity, technical accuracy, and reader usefulness in review. Maintain the guide as a project file. Change a rule when reviewed work demonstrates a better choice, then update its examples and checker configuration together. Related reading Reference while working Example writing guide — Read a complete project writing guide example.

documents.title: Evaluate agent tasks against your docs
documents.summary: Define realistic tasks, record reviewed answers from your own agent, and check the results against a documentation build.

headings.title: Prepare a report for the built site

documents.text: Use evaluation tasks to check whether an agent can accomplish important work using your documentation. Shoalrun defines task and result formats, prepares report templates, and checks those reports during an audit. You run your own agent and arrange human or external review of its answers. Shoalrun does not launch agents, choose a model, or grade prose. You need a built docs site, a few realistic tasks, and an agent or manual workflow for running them. The ordinary build does not execute evaluations or call a model. Evaluations are opt-in audit checks. Define a task file Save YAML or JSON with schemaVersion: 1 and a nonempty tasks list. Each task needs a unique lowercase ID, a prompt, an allowedTools list, and criteria with unique IDs and descriptions. Tasks are required by default; set required: false for an exploratory task that should not block an audit. evals/tasks.yaml schemaVersion : 1 tasks : - id : reader-views prompt : Explain what reader views hide and whether they protect private content. allowedTools : [ docs.search , docs.read ] criteria : - id : visibility description : Explain visibility versus access control and cite the reader-views page. - id : markdown description : Explain that published Markdown retains reader-marked content. Use the same tool names in your task file and runner report, such as search , fetch , docs.search , or mcp.get_page . Shoalrun validates the recorded runner tools against each executed task's allowed list. It cannot observe or enforce what tools an external agent actually used. Use a shared allowed tool set within a report; prepare separate suites for runs with different tool permissions. Write criteria that an expert can assess. Valid citations and complete report fields are mechanical checks. Whether the answer correctly explains your product remains a review judgment. Prepare a report for the built site shoalrun build docs.config.yaml site-dist shoalrun eval prepare site-dist --tasks evals/tasks.yaml --out evals/results.json Create the evals directory first. Preparation refuses to overwrite an existing report; use a new output filename for another run. The template contains a task-file digest, a documentation-build digest, a per-file buildFiles inventory, a timestamp, empty runner details, and each task marked skipped . It records no passing results and does not run the tasks. A template with skipped required tasks fails the check until you complete the run and review. The task digest uses normalized definitions, so whitespace-only changes do not invalidate a run. Prompt, criteria, tools, or required-status changes do. The build digest covers published output files, including HTML, Markdown, indexes, discovery, and assets. It excludes build-info.json , private ai/ artifacts, and .shoalrun/ state. File touches do not invalidate otherwise identical output; changed published bytes do. Other published metadata, including build IDs embedded in manifests, remains covered even when it reflects deployment provenance. Diagnose a different build Save a file inventory alongside an evaluation build: shoalrun eval snapshot site-dist > evaluated-build.json shoalrun eval snapshot rebuilt-site > current-build.json shoalrun eval compare current-build.json --since evaluated-build.json The comparison lists added, changed, and removed file paths. It exits 0 for identical snapshots and 1 for differences or invalid input. Each inventory binds relative file paths and SHA-256 byte digests to the same build digest used by evaluation reports. It contains no answers or grades. New report templates include this inventory in buildFiles . When a report is stale, eval check includes the file comparison in details.buildChanges . Older reports still receive the exact-build check, but cannot identify which earlier files differ. Editing the stored digest or deleting changed files is not a new evaluation. For local review of a hosted build, download and retain that exact output, task file, and report template. Run the tasks against the downloaded site and check the completed report against it. Rebuilding the source on another operating system can change rendered assets; a report about the downloaded build does not automatically cover that rebuild. Archive the source revision and build inventory with the run. A successful build capture records no evaluation pass. Run and review the tasks Use your own agent with the declared tool access. Record the actual runner name, optional model, available tools, and any limitations in runner . Replace recordedAt with the run's UTC ISO timestamp. For each task, record its status ( pass , fail , or skipped ), answer, citations, and criterion judgments. A passing result needs a nonempty answer, at least one citation, and a passing judgment with a reason for every defined criterion. Identify citations by stable page ID and publication, so editions and languages cannot be confused: { "taskId" : "reader-views" , "status" : "pass" , "answer" : "Reader views change visi

documents.summary: Complete, working docs.config.yaml files for common kinds of documentation sites.
documents.text: Each example below is a complete project in the repository's framework/example-configs/ directory, with pages and any OpenAPI files it needs. The test suite builds every one, and checks that the configs on this page match the files, so they stay correct. Start with the bundled minimal or api-docs project, then build it: shoalrun init my-docs --starter minimal cd my-docs shoalrun build docs.config.yaml site-dist shoalrun serve site-dist Use --starter api-docs for the Cedar Parcel API example. The other examples remain available to copy from framework/example-configs/ . The notifications project demonstrates an optional cookbook chooser with email, push, and SMS choices. Its YAML maps supported selections to prebuilt recipe pages. It also includes unpublished ingredient and recipe drafts to show the authoring path. Build it from the repository root: node framework/dist/cli.js build framework/example-configs/notifications/docs.config.yaml /tmp/notifications-site node framework/dist/cli.js serve /tmp/notifications-site The configuration reference explains every key. Minimal site One publication, page defaults so each page needs only an id , title , summary , and slug , and a two-level sidebar. example-configs/minimal/docs.config.yaml # The smallest useful site: one publication, two pages, a sidebar. schemaVersion : 1 site : title : Acme handbook publications : defaults : { channel : production , version : current , language : en } channels : production : { pathPrefix : "" } versions : current : { pathPrefix : "" } enabled : - { channel : production , version : current } # Every page gets these values unless it sets its own. frontmatter : defaults : type : guide channel : production version : current access : { policy : public } navigation : - id : welcome doc : guide.welcome - id : setup label : Setup items : - id : install doc : guide.install Parcel API documentation The fictional Cedar Parcel API demonstrates enrollment shapes, parcel filters, several response formats, binary uploads, deprecation, and a delivery webhook. documents.title: Focused OpenAPI contracts
documents.summary: Give tools one operation and its required schemas without the rest of the API source.

headings.title: What the export keeps and drops

documents.text: A focused contract is a generated OpenAPI JSON file for one operation. It contains that operation's path and method, parameters, request and response definitions, named examples, and the schemas and security schemes those definitions use. The build resolves local references so the file stands on its own. Each API reference page links to its focused contract. Why use one An API reference page is made for reading. A focused contract gives an agent, test tool, or client generator the exact machine-readable shape of the operation. A large OpenAPI source can contain many unrelated operations and schemas; the focused file keeps the context to what this operation needs. It is also useful when the full source should stay internal but a selected operation can be published. Generate and inspect it Set focused: true on a local API source. The source can stay unpublished: config/api.yaml notes : source : kind : file path : ../apis/notes/openapi.yaml focused : true operations : - id : notes.create sourceOperationId : createNote reference : reference.create-note The build writes a JSON file under /api/operations/ and links to it from the API reference page. If publish: true also publishes the source OpenAPI file, the focused contract is generated automatically. Open the Create a note reference , then follow its Download JSON link to inspect the output from this site's fictional API. That site's full OpenAPI source is published too, so you can compare them. Before a normal build publishes the contract, review the local candidate and pin the API's publicReview.digest as described in API references . The review covers the contract's transitive schemas and examples as well as the page that links to it. The focused contract describes the selected operation, not the entire API. Use the full source when a tool needs operations outside that page. What the export keeps and drops It keeps the selected path and method, their parameters, and the schemas, examples, and security schemes they reference. The root servers and security carry over, and tags lists only the operation's tags. It drops every x-* extension key, so vendor extensions and internal notes stored there stay out of the public file. It supports local OpenAPI 3.0.x and 3.1.x files with internal and multi-file references. Referenced files must stay inside the main OpenAPI file's directory, including after resolving symlinks. Absolute local paths are rejected. A Path Item $ref , or a JSON Schema $id , $anchor , $dynamicRef , or $dynamicAnchor , stops the build. The URL pattern is /api/operations/<channel>/<version>/<language>/<name>-<sha256>.json . The suffix is the full SHA-256 of the generated JSON bytes. Changing the contract changes its URL; an unchanged contract keeps the same URL. Earlier prototype filenames hashed the operation ID, which did not provide this property. The generated hosting metadata gives these URLs Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable and a strong ETag containing the same digest. The Node server applies these headers, and the Vercel adapter includes them in its routing configuration. A CDN can replace the ETag with its own validator. Use the returned ETag for conditional requests and the manifest's focusedContractDigest to verify downloaded bytes. Mutable Markdown and JSON indexes require revalidation. Other hosts must apply the generated cache policy. Old builds are not archived automatically, so the URL identity does not guarantee permanent availability. To check every contract in a built site, run shoalrun api focused-audit <site-directory> . The CLI reference lists what it checks. Related reading Reference while working CLI reference — Check every focused contract in a built site with api focused-audit. Related topics Agent-friendly documentation — Focused contracts are how agents find exact API details without the full spec.

If publish: true also publishes the source OpenAPI file, the focused contract is generated automatically. Open the Create a note reference , then follow its Download JSON link to inspect the output from this site's fictional API. That site's full OpenAPI source is published too, so you can compare them. Before a normal build publishes the contract, review the local candidate and pin the API's publicReview.digest as described in API references . The review covers the contract's transitive schemas and examples as well as the page that links to it. The focused contract describes the selected operation, not the entire API. Use the full source when a tool needs operations outside that page. What the export keeps and drops It keeps the selected path and method, their parameters, and the schemas, examples, and security schemes they reference. The root servers and security carry over, and tags lists only the operation's tags. It drops every x-* extension key, so vendor extensions and internal notes stored there stay out of the public file. It supports local OpenAPI 3.0.x and 3.1.x files with internal and multi-file references. Referenced files must stay inside the main OpenAPI file's directory, including after resolving symlinks. Absolute local paths are rejected. A Path Item $ref , or a JSON Schema $id , $anchor , $dynamicRef , or $dynamicAnchor , stops the build. The URL pattern is /api/operations/<channel>/<version>/<language>/<name>-<sha256>.json . The suffix is the full SHA-256 of the generated JSON bytes. Changing the contract changes its URL; an unchanged contract keeps the same URL. Earlier prototype filenames hashed the operation ID, which did not provide this property. The generated hosting metadata gives these URLs Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable and a strong ETag containing the same digest. The Node server applies these headers, and the Vercel adapter includes them in its routing configuration. A CDN can replace the ETag with its own validator. Use the returned ETag for conditional requests and the manifest's focusedContractDigest to verify downloaded bytes. Mutable Markdown and JSON indexes require revalidation. Other hosts must apply the generated cache policy. Old builds are not archived automatically, so the URL identity does not guarantee permanent availability. To check every contract in a built site, run shoalrun api focused-audit <site-directory> . The CLI reference lists what it checks. Related reading Reference while working CLI reference — Check every focused contract in a built site with api focused-audit. Related topics
Agent-friendly documentation — Focused contracts are how agents find exact API details without the full spec.

documents.title: Site footer
documents.summary: Add link columns, a bottom row of links, and a short text line below every page.
documents.text: The footer sits below every page, after the navigation and article. Configure it under site.footer . Without that setting, the site has no footer. docs.config.yaml site : title : Example documentation footer : columns : - title : Guides links : - { label : Get started , href : /start } - { label : Authentication , href : /guides/auth } - title : Company links : - { label : Status , href : "https://status.example.com" } - { label : Contact support , href : "mailto:support@example.com" } links : - { label : Privacy , href : /legal/privacy } - { label : Terms , href : /legal/terms } text : © 2026 Example, Inc. Columns appear first, side by side on wide screens and stacked on phones. Below them, a bottom row shows text on the left and links on the right. Every part is optional, but the footer needs at least one of them. Footer settings These settings configure the footer text and its links. Setting Required Value columns No A list of link groups. Each has a title and a links list with at least one link. links No Links for the bottom row, such as legal pages. text No One line of plain text, such as a copyright notice. The build escapes it, so HTML and Markdown show as typed. Each link takes a label and an href . An href is a site-root path such as /start , an http or https URL, or a mailto: link. External http and https links get rel="noopener" . The build rejects any other URL scheme, including javascript: . Footer links don't take a style . Use header links for buttons and calls to action. Layout and themes The footer uses the page's theme tokens, so each theme preset and palette restyles it. On landing and splash layouts , it matches the narrower landing width. The CSS and theme reference lists its classes. The footer is part of the HTML page only. Markdown twins, search results, and /llms.txt do not include it. Related reading No matching documents.

documents.text: This is the field inventory for this documentation site. The tables below are built from Shoalrun's native field definitions and this site's frontmatter.fields declarations on each build. They describe source page headers, not the shorter YAML header selected for a published Markdown page. agent.intent in the project-defined table is an optional string. This site's authors use it to describe the task a page helps an agent complete. It is not a required Shoalrun field or an instruction to an agent. editorial.reviewNote is another site-specific field for internal review notes. A different project can declare different fields. To publish an equivalent inventory on your site, place <FrontmatterReference /> on a page. It takes no attributes or child content and renders the current project's native and declared fields in HTML and Markdown. Identify and route a page Use the page ID for links and cards that should survive a URL change. The slug supplies the page part of the URL; publication prefixes may be added around it. Summary is short preview text; description is a separate, optional fuller account. Project output rules choose which field supplies each surface. Field Type Needed What it changes id string On each page Stable page identity used by document links and cards; keep it when the file or URL changes. title string After inheritance Page heading and default browser title. summary string After inheritance Short page preview, used by cards and other configured text surfaces. description string Optional Fuller description of what the page covers; kept distinct from the short summary. type string After inheritance Document kind, such as guide or api-reference; can select a Markdown metadata profile. slug string On each page Page URL path before channel, version, and language prefixes. Choose a publication and visibility The project enables specific channel/version/language combinations. A page is built only for combinations matching its resolved values. audiences and readerFilters select reader views when the site config enables them; access.policy determines whether the page enters this public build. A draft page is excluded. Field Type Needed What it changes channel string Public page Publication environment, such as sandbox or production; selects an enabled publication and API source. version string Public page API or documentation edition, such as v1; selects an enabled publication and API source. language string Optional Content language; uses frontmatter defaults/enforced values, then publications.defaults.language, then en. locale string Optional Formatting conventions used in the content; can inherit a project locale for the page language and can be overridden per page. access object Public page Controls whether the page enters a public build; this object is not exported to Markdown metadata. access.policy string With access Use public to publish this page; draft pages are excluded from the built site. audiences array Optional Readers this page is intended for; does not control who can access it. readerFilters object Optional Configured reader filter choices for this page. Missing facets are shared. Language is the content language and selects a publication. Locale describes formatting conventions in the content and does not select a publication. frontmatter.locales can set a project locale for each language; pages may override it. Categorize, connect, and present the page product , area , and subarea are optional, nonempty string categories. They can come from project defaults and appear in the document manifest and search index. A matching configured reader facet makes each category a page filter; without that facet it remains taxonomy only. operations links a guide or reference to stable API operation IDs. On a guide or how-to page, relatedApiReferences names API reference page IDs to add cross links in both directions within the same publication. Tags help document collections find the page. Card settings change its preview when another page links to it; they do not change the destination. subjectLifecycle displays the status of the documented API or feature; lifecycle is available for the document's editorial state. tocDepth limits the HTML page table of contents; use 0 to hide it. layout picks the HTML page layout: docs , wide , landing , or splash . showNavigationTabs overrides the navigation tab bar for this page; landing and splash pages hide it by default. image replaces the generated link-preview image. date and releaseVersion can identify a changelog entry under the project's frontmatter.changelogIdentifier rule. Field Type Needed What it changes product string Optional Optional product category. Also selects the product reader facet when that facet is configured. area string Optional Optional area category. Also selects the area reader facet when that facet is configured. subarea string Optional Optional finer category. Also selects the subarea reader facet when that facet is config

documents.text: Frontmatter is the YAML header between the first two --- lines of a .md or .mdx page. It gives a page its identity, URL, and publication settings. Start with this complete header, then write the page body below it: --- id : guide.first-page title : Your first page summary : Create and publish a page in your documentation site. type : guide slug : /first-page channel : production version : current language : en access : { policy : public } --- Keep id stable when you rename a file or change its URL. Use it in navigation and links such as [Your first page](doc:guide.first-page) . To try the full workflow, add a page . See the generated frontmatter reference under Write documentation for native and project-defined fields. Each build also writes .shoalrun/frontmatter-reference.md and .shoalrun/frontmatter.schema.json beside docs.config.yaml for local authoring. Required after inheritance These fields identify a page and give it a route. id is the durable target for links and cards; slug is the URL path and may change without breaking those references. summary is short preview text. The optional description can explain the page more fully. A project chooses which field supplies each output surface. The five fields in this table must exist after the compiler combines the page header with project-wide values. Only id and slug must always be written in the page itself. For instance, the project can set a default type: guide while each page keeps its own identity and URL. Field Type Purpose id string Stable identity; keep it when the filename, title, or URL changes. title string Page heading and default HTML title. summary string Short preview for cards and other configured surfaces. type string Document kind, such as guide or api-reference . slug string Explicit URL path before publication prefixes. These related fields are optional: Field Type Purpose description string Fuller account of what the page covers. updated string Last meaningful revision date; an opt-in digest history can derive it from content changes. verified string Author-set YYYY-MM-DD date when the technical claims were checked; independent of Updated. date string Publication date in YYYY-MM-DD form; can identify a changelog entry. releaseVersion string Product release label; can identify a changelog entry. Separate from version . Publication fields Publication fields identify the channel, version, language, and access policy for a page. Field Type Purpose channel string Publication channel, such as sandbox or production . version string API or documentation version. publications list of { channel, version } Publish one source page in several channel/version combinations. Use instead of page-level channel and version . language string Optional content language; resolved from globals, publication defaults, then en . locale string Optional conventions used for dates, numbers, and currency in the content; does not select a publication. access.policy string Set to public for a public page. Channel identifies an environment such as sandbox or production; version identifies an API or documentation edition; language identifies the content language. The resolved combination must be enabled in project config. channel , version , and access can come from global frontmatter. A language on the page overrides the default unless the project enforces one. For an unchanged page that belongs in v1 and v2, replace its page-level channel and version with: publications : - { channel : production , version : v1 } - { channel : production , version : v2 } Each entry must name a declared channel and version, and the pairs must be unique. Only enabled combinations publish. One source file uses one language; write a translated file for another language. To vary just part of a shared page, use <ForPublication version="v2"> as shown in share pages across versions . Publishing policy access.policy controls whether a page is included in the generated site. Write it in the page's YAML header as access: { policy: public } when the page is ready to publish. New pages created by shoalrun scaffold start with access: { policy: draft } so you can finish them before publishing. Policy Build result public Published if the page also matches an enabled channel, version, and language. draft Checked for valid frontmatter, but omitted from the site. Only public publishes a page; other policy strings are treated like drafts. This setting controls build output, not reader sign-in or permissions. A site's global frontmatter.defaults.access can supply a policy for pages that omit it. Global defaults and enforced values Set shared values under frontmatter.defaults in docs.config.yaml . Page values override defaults; frontmatter.enforced overrides page values. Objects merge recursively and arrays replace. Keep id and slug on each page. docs.config.yaml frontmatter : defaults : type : guide channel : production version : current access : { policy : draft } An explicit page policy of public p

documents.title: Glossary
documents.summary: Look up documentation, publishing, search, and agent terminology, with links to the relevant guides.
documents.text: This page defines the terms used across Shoalrun's documentation. Look a term up when a guide uses a word you don't know. Terms are sorted A to Z, and each definition links to the full guide. Filter the list by a term or a word in its definition, for example publication or agent . In the Markdown version, use your reader's Find command. To see how the main terms fit together, read How Shoalrun works . Filter terms and definitions $concat A directive that adds items to a list inherited through extends . See Configuration reference . $include A directive that replaces a value with the contents of another YAML file. Paths are relative to the file that uses it. See Configuration reference . $remove A directive that drops inherited mapping keys, or list items by id . It fails when nothing is inherited. See Configuration reference . Access policy The access.policy field. public puts a page in the build. Any other value, such as draft , keeps it out. It does not control who can read a published page. See Page metadata . AFDocs An external scorecard for agent-friendly documentation used in development checks. See Agent-friendly documentation . Agent intent A self-reported category describing why an agent called an MCP tool. Optional analytics can record allowed categories; it does not reveal private model reasoning. See MCP analytics . Agent skill Packaged instructions that help an existing agent set up or maintain a Shoalrun project. A skill guides the workflow; documentation tools provide reference lookups. See Bundled agent skills . Alt text Text describing an image for readers who cannot see it. <Image> requires alt ; alt="" marks a decorative image for screen readers to skip. See Images . Analytics adapter A project module that sends supported browser or MCP events to your chosen service. Each integration is optional and off by default. See browser analytics and MCP analytics . Answer cache Temporary storage for checked answers in a running chat server. Matching repeated questions can reuse them while their source passages remain current. It is separate from prepared answer cards. See Answer checks and reuse . Answer card A reviewed answer to a common question, generated ahead of time with shoalrun answers using a chat model. A confirmed match serves it without a new chat-model answer, though matching uses an embedding provider and scorer. It is not a page-preview card. See Prepared answers . API catalog The /.well-known/api-catalog file, a linkset that points an API endpoint to its OpenAPI description. It needs a discovery endpoint and the site origin. See Agent-friendly documentation . ApiExample A component that copies a named example from an OpenAPI source into a guide. See ApiExample and ApiSchema . ApiSchema A component that includes a request body, response body, object, or single field from an OpenAPI source. See ApiExample and ApiSchema . API source An entry in apis that points to a local OpenAPI file. kind: file is the only supported kind. See Add an OpenAPI API . Audit The shoalrun audit command. It runs configured tests, audits OpenAPI sources, builds the site, and checks focused contracts. See Audit a docs project . Authored reference An API reference page you write in MDX. The build adds the operation details below your text. See Add an OpenAPI API . Authoring guidance Project editorial instructions, writing-guide paths, and reviewed examples that help an agent follow team conventions. See writing guides . Automatic footer A list that the build adds to the end of a page without a relationship. Examples are Related documentation and Related API references. See Related reading . Base path The site.basePath setting. It prefixes public page and resource URLs, including assets, search, API downloads, and discovery files. See Configuration reference . Build The shoalrun build command. It compiles a site into an output directory and replaces that directory. See CLI reference . Build provenance The /build-info.json file. It records the config digest and, when you pass them, a source commit and release label. See Publishing and agent representations . Bundled docs The documentation snapshot shipped with an installed Shoalrun package. Local CLI reads and the local documentation MCP server use it without fetching the live site. See CLI reference . Callout A component that highlights a short message. It has a type and an optional label. See Callouts . Callout tone The line, background, and text colors of a callout type. Five tones are built in, and you can register more. See Callouts . Callout type The purpose of a callout: note , tip , important , warning , caution , or a type you register. See Callouts . Card A linked preview of another page. It shows the target's title and summary and follows the target's current URL. It is not an answer card . See Cards and collections . Changelog identifier The frontmatter.changelogIdentifier rule. It decides whether a changelog entry is identified by date, release

documents.title: Header links
documents.summary: Add links and buttons to the site masthead.
documents.text: The masthead shows the site title, the publication label, the search box , the dark mode toggle when it's on, and any links you configure. Add links under site.header.links : docs.config.yaml site : title : Example documentation header : links : - { label : Guides , href : /start } - { label : GitHub , href : "https://github.com/example/project" , style : button } - { label : Get started , href : /start , style : primary } Links appear in list order, after the search box and toggle. Link settings Use these settings to configure each link shown in the header. Setting Required Value label Yes Visible link text. href Yes A site-root path such as /start , an http or https URL, or a mailto: link. style No link (default), button , or primary . link renders as plain text. button has an outline. primary fills with --color-accent and uses --color-accent-contrast for its text. Use one primary link at most, for the action you most want readers to take. External http and https links get rel="noopener" . The build rejects any other URL scheme, including javascript: . Layout and themes On narrow screens, the search box and links wrap onto their own row below the site title. Each theme preset restyles them to match its shape. The CSS and theme reference lists their classes. Header links are part of the HTML page only. Markdown twins and /llms.txt do not include them. Related reading Reference while working CSS and theme reference — Look up the header classes each preset styles. Related topics Light and dark mode — The dark mode toggle appears in the header beside your links. Site search — The search box sits in the site header, before your header links.

documents.title: Shoalrun
documents.summary: A preview of Shoalrun, a flexible framework for API and product docs with fine-grained controls for what people see and what agents can discover and read.

documents.text: Docs for people. Context for agents. One source, with control over how each audience reads it. Build interactive docs for people and readable content for agents, with checks before you publish. See what an agent gets See what works today Prototype preview: Explore the docs today. Shoalrun's compiler and CLI are still a private prototype, so installation isn't available yet. See what works today → Readable output, with checks you can inspect Write Markdown, MDX, and OpenAPI once. People get tabs, disclosures, navigation, and reader views. Agents get the supported content in reading order, with stable page identities and machine-readable contracts. What you can inspect What it gives you A manifest with byte digests Stable page IDs and publication variants, with SHA-256 digests for checking the exact Markdown bytes. Compact discovery and incremental sync Find a page without the full search index; compare saved snapshots when a build changes. Focused per-operation OpenAPI contracts One small contract containing an operation and the local schemas it needs, when enabled. Explicit component representations Tabs and disclosures become labeled sections. Snippets expand into their resolved content. Unsupported components fail the build. Reader views and format-specific content Choose what people see in the browser and write different explanations for HTML and Markdown when needed. A tabbed page, without missing panels This example has two client choices and a closed disclosure. The Markdown includes both clients and the troubleshooting detail. The full manifest supplies byte digests when you need verification; build information and sync snapshots let returning clients detect changes. documents.title: Add Shoalrun to another build or host
documents.summary: Publish compiled files alongside another site and supply the host's HTTP rules.
documents.text: Shoalrun builds a complete static site without a host framework. To include its pages in another build system, run Shoalrun's CLI as a build step. Then copy the generated files into the host's output. The host does not need to parse Shoalrun's MDX or OpenAPI sources. shoalrun build docs.config.yaml ./shoalrun-dist The command replaces ./shoalrun-dist on each build. Use a dedicated output directory. With an empty site.basePath , copy its contents to the root of the host's published output. For a site mounted at /docs , set site.basePath: /docs and copy the public shoalrun-dist/docs/ subtree to the host's /docs mount. The build also keeps internal manifests at the output root for local commands. Add a build adapter An adapter for Astro, another site builder, or a deployment platform can follow these steps: Run shoalrun build <config> <temporary-output> after the host has generated its own files. Enumerate both output trees and fail if a Shoalrun file would replace a host file. Also fail if a file occupies a directory the other tree needs. Compare paths without regard to case so a build that works on one filesystem does not overwrite files on another. Copy the Shoalrun files into the host output, keeping their paths. Do not modify the generated HTML or Markdown: both came from the same content build. Configure the host's routing and response headers as described below. Run the post-deploy checker against the published URL. The generated documents.json lists every page's HTML and Markdown URLs. redirects.json records redirects, and resource-headers.json records content types for Markdown and discovery resources. It also records Content-Security-Policy: sandbox and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff for generated and local SVG files. Apply those headers when hosting SVGs; the Node server and Vercel adapter do this automatically. /llms.txt , search-index.json , API contracts, images, styles, and scripts are ordinary output files. The output guide lists their paths. Supply HTTP behavior Copying files does not make a static host negotiate Markdown at an HTML URL or apply redirects and special content types. Use the content negotiation contract to configure those rules. A host that cannot inspect request headers can still serve the direct .md URLs, but cannot provide the negotiated response. Shoalrun's Node server handles these rules; the Vercel build generates a deployable configuration for that host. Keep the adapter small: Shoalrun owns content compilation and the generated files, while the host owns request handling. A JavaScript plugin API is not required to call the CLI or publish its output. Related reading Next steps Check a deployed site — Confirm the host applies the HTTP rules correctly. Related topics Deploy your documentation — Apply the hosting contract on another platform. Publish on Vercel — The Vercel build generates its own HTTP rules; other hosts need them supplied.
