documents.title: Host and limit documentation chat
documents.summary: Deploy chat on Vercel with shared usage limits, a visitor challenge, optional logs, and an off switch.
documents.text: Host chat after testing it locally . The Vercel function runs beside the documentation site and needs shared usage limits. You can also add a visitor challenge, question logging, and an immediate pause switch. Before building the hosted function, have these ready: Chat and embedding configuration, with the provider keys available in the required environments. A shared store that speaks the Upstash REST API. A Vercel project and the public address in site.origin . The normal site build does not add this function. Hosted provider requests can incur costs. Cap the daily spend chat.budget limits how many questions can reach a chat model each day. These are question limits, not a currency cap; one question can involve several model calls, and embedding or scoring requests are separate. docs.config.yaml chat : budget : { perCaller : 40 , perDay : 1000 } Setting What it does perCaller The most questions one caller can send to the model in a day. perDay The most the whole site can send in a day. It must be at least perCaller . store Where the counters live. Leave it out for memory, or name a shared store. See below. A request reserves one slot before answering. If no chat-model call is made, the slot is returned. Cached answers and excerpts can still be served when the model budget is spent; retrieval or scoring can have their own provider costs. A question that needs a new answer gets links to the closest pages instead. Counters reset at midnight UTC. Each function instance keeps its own cache in memory, so a repeat can still reach the model when another instance answered it first. Answer cards can serve common questions without a new chat-model answer when you generate them into the function's private index before deployment. Identify callers The handler tells callers apart with the clientKey function you give it, such as one that reads the address from a request header. It stores only a hash of the value. Without clientKey , every caller shares one cap. If the counter store fails, the model counts as spent, so an outage can't open it up. Use a shared store With no store , the counters live in memory. They reset when the server restarts and aren't shared between processes, which suits the local preview. A serverless host runs many instances, so it needs a store they all share. store names one that speaks the Upstash REST API, which Upstash Redis and Vercel KV both provide. docs.config.yaml chat : budget : perCaller : 40 perDay : 1000 store : { provider : upstash , urlEnv : KV_REST_API_URL , tokenEnv : KV_REST_API_TOKEN } urlEnv and tokenEnv name the environment variables that hold the address and token, and the config never holds either. A missing variable, a slow store, or a store that returns an error counts as a spent budget. The chat then shows the closest pages and never opens up. Shoalrun prints the reason once to the server log. The store address must use https , and a request that takes more than two seconds fails without a retry. For a caller key on a host, use clientKeyFromHeader with a header the host sets, such as x-vercel-forwarded-for . On a host that passes that header through, a caller can forge it and start a fresh personal cap. The site-wide cap still holds. Because a slot is taken before the answer and not counted after, questions that arrive together can't all get past a cap. If answering fails, the slot stays taken, because the model may already have been paid. Host the chat on Vercel The chat can run as a Vercel function on the same deployment as the site. It is optional, and a build never adds it unless you ask. Add --chat to the Vercel build: shoalrun vercel build docs.config.yaml .vercel/output --chat The build indexes the site and puts the index inside the function's own directory, never in the public static files. It writes the chat settings, without any key, and copies the code the function needs. The function answers at /__shoalrun/ask . If the function cannot be added, the build fails with a reason. Check for: A missing chat or retrieval.embeddings section. A missing chat.budget.store . An embedding key unavailable during the build. What the function needs The function refuses to start without a shared budget store, because counters kept by each server instance would limit nothing. You name the environment variables that hold your keys, and the config never holds a value. Variable Used for VOYAGE_API_KEY (or the variable retrieval.embeddings.keyEnv names) Embedding the passages at build time, and each question at run time. The variable chat.keyEnv names The chat model. JEV_API_KEY (or the variable chat.rerank.keyEnv names) A configured relevance scorer. Without its key, that scorer counts as down. The two variables chat.budget.store names The shared store. Vercel KV adds KV_REST_API_URL and KV_REST_API_TOKEN for you. The variable chat.challenge.secretEnv names The Turnstile secret. Only requests to the site's own addresses are accepted: the production host from site.origin , the depl

documents.title: Audit the Shoalrun docs project
documents.summary: Run configured project checks and inspect failures before sharing a change.
documents.text: Run Shoalrun's configured checks. This repository's formatting check requires Vale 3.20 or newer: npx --no-install shoalrun audit docs/docs.config.yaml The audit checks configured project commands, API representations, and focused contracts. Read any reported finding and fix its source before continuing. This command does not run the complete framework test suite or replace a browser review. Framework source changes and tests belong in the framework repository.

documents.title: Build the Shoalrun docs site
documents.summary: Compile authored documentation into local HTML, Markdown, and manifests.
documents.text: Use the installed CLI to build Shoalrun's documentation: npx --no-install shoalrun build docs/docs.config.yaml docs/dist The source configuration is docs/docs.config.yaml ; output goes to docs/dist . The root shortcut is npm run docs:build ; it uses the installed package. If the build fails, fix the named source or configuration issue and rerun it. A previous successful output can remain on disk after a failure, so file existence alone is not evidence of a successful new build.

documents.title: Install the site dependencies
documents.summary: Install the pinned Shoalrun package and this site’s declared dependencies.
documents.text: Install the versions pinned by this site’s lockfile: npm ci npx --no-install shoalrun config validate docs/docs.config.yaml This site pins a private registry package in its manifest and lockfile. documents.title: Check the built page artifacts
documents.summary: Resolve a document ID through the manifest and check its HTML and Markdown files.
documents.text: Choose a document by its stable ID. The default below checks the recipes overview; replace it with the ID of the page you changed. export DOC_ID = "${DOC_ID :- guide.recipes-overview}" node --input-type=module << 'JS' import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises'; import path from 'node:path'; const root = 'docs/dist'; const manifest = JSON.parse(await readFile(path.join(root, 'documents.json'), 'utf8')); const doc = manifest.documents.find(item => item.id === process.env.DOC_ID); if (!doc) throw new Error(`No published document with ID ${process.env.DOC_ID}`); for (const route of [`${doc.url.replace(/\/$/, '')}/index.html`, doc.markdownUrl]) { const file = path.join(root, route.replace(/^\//, '')); if (!(await readFile(file, 'utf8')).trim()) throw new Error(`Empty output: ${file}`); console.log(file); } JS If the ID is missing, check the page's access policy and publication fields, then rebuild. Inspect the printed Markdown file for the expected instructions. Use a local HTTP preview for the HTML page so its assets and navigation resolve correctly.

documents.title: Page layouts, landing pages, and splash pages
documents.summary: Give a page more width, or build a landing or full-bleed splash page with a Hero and Sections, using the layout frontmatter field.
documents.text: Every page uses the docs layout unless its frontmatter sets layout . Layouts change the HTML page only. The Markdown twin, search, and llms.txt stay the same. Layout Sidebar On this page Use it for docs Yes Yes Guides and reference pages. This is the default. wide Yes No Wide tables, diagrams, and API overviews that need the full content width. landing No No Home pages and product entry points. A Hero replaces the page header. splash No No Marketing pages built from full-width bands. A Hero replaces the page header, and Section blocks stack edge to edge. Frontmatter layout : wide An unknown value fails the build. Each preset styles all four layouts, and project CSS can target one through html[data-layout="wide"] , html[data-layout="landing"] , or html[data-layout="splash"] . Control navigation tabs The built-in layouts are docs , wide , landing , and splash . There is no custom layout value; use landing or splash for a custom entry page and style it with project CSS. When the site config defines navigation tabs, docs and wide pages show the section bar by default. Landing and splash pages hide it by default. Override that choice on any page: Frontmatter layout : splash showNavigationTabs : false Set showNavigationTabs: true to include the tab bar on a landing or splash page. Set it to false to suppress it on a docs or wide page. The value must be a boolean and can also come from frontmatter defaults or enforced values. With no configured tabs, neither value creates a bar. This setting affects the HTML section bar only. It does not change the page's sidebar, tab membership, breadcrumbs, Markdown, search records, or agent indexes. An agent can still discover and read every published section without visiting the homepage. Build a landing page Set layout: landing , then open the page with a Hero . To serve the page at the site root, give it slug: / . When a page has slug: / , the site title in the masthead links to it. This example is a small landing page: content/home.mdx --- id : guide.home title : Shoalrun summary : Payments for small teams, in five lines of code. type : overview slug : / layout : landing access : { policy : public } --- < Hero tagline = "Take your first payment in five lines of code." > [ Start building ](doc:guide.overview) [ See how it works ](doc:guide.concepts) </ Hero > ## Start here < DocCards docs = {[ "guide.overview" , "guide.concepts" , "guide.api-references" ]} /> Hero Hero opens a landing page with a large title, a tagline, and up to three action buttons. It can also show an image or a code block beside the text. Attribute Required Meaning tagline Yes One or two sentences under the title. title No The large title. Defaults to the page title . align No center (default) or start , which aligns the title, tagline, and buttons to the left. image No An https URL, or a local .png , .jpg , .webp , or .svg file relative to the page file. imageAlt With image What the image shows. Use imageAlt="" when the image is decorative. Put the actions in the body as ordinary Markdown links, one per line or as a list. The first link is the primary button. doc: links resolve by page ID, like everywhere else. Show an image or code Add image and imageAlt to show a picture beside the text. The build copies a local image to /assets/pages/<page path>/ . < Hero tagline = "Payments in five lines of code." image = "./images/dashboard.png" imageAlt = "The payments dashboard showing today's volume" > [ Get started ](doc:guide.start) </ Hero > Or put one fenced code block in the body. It appears in an editor-style window with its title and a Copy button, and keeps the site's code colors. The home page of this site uses one. < Hero tagline = "Build API documentation from Markdown, MDX, and OpenAPI." > [ Start building ](doc:guide.overview) ``` sh title="Build and preview this site" npm ci --prefix framework npm run docs:dev ``` </ Hero > With an image or code block, the hero splits into two columns, text first, and aligns to the left. Below 60rem wide, the visual moves under the text. A hero can show an image or a code block, not both. Rules Hero needs layout: landing or layout: splash , and it replaces the page header, including the Read as Markdown link. Put it first on the page. Attributes are literal text. The body can contain only action links and one code block; other content fails the build. In the Markdown twin, Hero becomes the tagline, a list of its links, then its image (when imageAlt isn't empty) or its code block. A custom title that differs from the page title appears in bold before the tagline. Landing pages are centered and at most 76rem wide, and the masthead lines up with them. On a phone, the hero stacks its buttons. Build a splash page A splash page is a marketing page. Set layout: splash , open with a Hero , then build the rest from Section blocks. The layout removes the sidebar, the outline, and the content padding, so the hero and each section run ed

documents.summary: Update Shoalrun's agent workflows and the generated documentation they consult.
documents.text: Shoalrun's portable skills live in framework/skills/ . To use them on a site, see use the bundled agent skills . This page covers changing the workflows shipped with Shoalrun. Validate a skill change Edit the relevant SKILL.md and any supporting files in its folder. Keep commands consistent with the CLI reference and verify the workflow against a temporary project. From the repository root, with skill-validator installed, run: skill-validator check --strict framework/skills/shoalrun-setup skill-validator check --strict framework/skills/shoalrun-author skill-validator check --strict framework/skills/shoalrun-recipes skill-validator check --strict framework/skills/shoalrun-walkthrough Validation checks the skill structure. Review its instructions and execute the affected workflow as well. Refresh the documentation bundle The CLI's docs search and docs read commands consult generated files under framework/agent-docs/ : documents.json maps stable page IDs to publication variants and Markdown paths. search-index.json contains searchable page records. The .md files contain complete generated pages. The authored source is docs/content/ . After changing those sources, run from the repository root: npm run agent-docs:build npm test Commit the generated changes with the source changes. The suite compares the bundle with a fresh site build, including its search index and page content. documents.title: Markdown metadata
documents.summary: Public field projection, source paths, profiles, precedence, and required values.

headings.title: Put a field on every page
Declare sections that can be read alone

documents.text: The build publishes the page metadata guide as Markdown alongside its HTML page. That .md file starts with a YAML header containing selected values from the source page header. Source headers can grow long and contain review notes or other details that do not help an agent read the page. Selecting a small set of useful fields keeps the agent's context focused and avoids exposing internal metadata in that header. Compare the two custom values in that guide's source: docs/content/frontmatter.mdx agent : intent : Help authors understand and configure page metadata. editorial : reviewNote : Check the frontmatter examples before release. The generated .md header includes agent.intent but leaves out editorial.reviewNote : docs/dist/author/frontmatter.md --- id : guide.frontmatter title : Page metadata summary : Set page identity, publication, and presentation fields before publishing. description : Learn how page metadata, project defaults, and publication choices shape the site and its Markdown output. type : reference audiences : - authors - maintainers canonical : /author/frontmatter agent : intent : Help authors understand and configure page metadata. --- The agent.intent value appears because this site's docs/docs.config.yaml selects it for reference pages. The relevant settings are: docs/docs.config.yaml outputs : markdown : metadata : format : yaml-frontmatter fields : id : frontmatter.id title : frontmatter.title summary : frontmatter.summary description : frontmatter.description type : frontmatter.type audiences : frontmatter.audiences subjectLifecycle : frontmatter.subjectLifecycle canonical : publication.canonicalUrl omitNull : true byType : reference : addFields : agent.intent : frontmatter.agent.intent Each entry under fields names an output key on the left and its source on the right. Here summary and description stay separate, while audiences comes from the page's intended-reader labels. The byType.reference rule adds agent.intent only for pages whose type is reference . subjectLifecycle is absent from the example output because that guide has no subjectLifecycle value and omitNull is true. The review note is absent because its declaration sets public: false and the output config does not select it. This controls only the generated YAML header: text written in the page body still appears in the published Markdown and HTML. Keep this header short. Include the fields an agent needs for the page, and leave out long descriptions or notes that take up its context. Projection settings format must be yaml-frontmatter to write a header. It defaults to none , so a projection with fields but no format writes no header and reports no error. format: none removes the header while leaving the full page body in Markdown. A field source is either frontmatter.<path> or one of these publication values: Source Value publication.channel The page's publication channel. publication.version The page's publication version. publication.language The page's language. publication.canonicalUrl The page route, such as /author/frontmatter . It is site-relative, not an absolute URL. Built-in public fields can be selected directly. A custom field needs a declaration with public: true . The protected roots access , seo , markdownMetadata , variables , tocDepth , private , internal , card , and displayText cannot be selected under any name. With omitNull: false , a missing value fails the build instead of being skipped. Layers apply in order. The base settings come first, then byType.<type> , then a named profile, then the page's own override. Each layer accepts format , fields , addFields , removeFields , and omitNull . fields replaces the inherited fields; addFields merges into them; removeFields drops output names and fails if a name is missing. Define named profiles under profiles , then select one from a page: docs.config.yaml outputs : markdown : metadata : format : yaml-frontmatter fields : { id : frontmatter.id , title : frontmatter.title } profiles : minimal : removeFields : [ title ] A page's frontmatter markdownMetadata : minimal A page can also write the override as a mapping, such as markdownMetadata: { profile: minimal, addFields: { language: publication.language } } . The example API project under framework/example/ uses the same declaration and projection pattern. See the generated frontmatter reference for the local project field inventory. See cards and collections for card inheritance and collection filters, and related reading for authored reading paths. Put a field on every page List the field under fields at the top level of outputs.markdown.metadata . Top-level fields apply to every page. A byType rule adds fields only for pages of that type, so use it for extras and not for a field that every page needs. To require the value as well, declare the field with required: true . A page that lacks it then fails the build, and the error names the file: docs.config.yaml frontmatter : fields : agent.intent :

documents.title: Measure MCP tool usage
documents.summary: Send optional server events to your analytics service without changing the documentation tools.

headings.title: Optionally identify the client and model
Optionally collect intent and group calls
Enable the adapter and verify an event

documents.text: Add a server adapter to measure calls to your HTTP MCP endpoint . Analytics is off by default. Enabling MCP does not enable tracking, and the browser analytics setting does not count tool calls. Your adapter chooses the service and sends the events. Shoalrun packages it for Node or the generated Vercel function. This setting does not instrument stdio, direct Markdown requests, or browser page views. Enable analytics Add your server adapter to the MCP configuration. documents.title: Connect an MCP client
documents.summary: Connect read-only MCP clients over stdio or HTTP to search and read built documentation.

headings.title: Why offer MCP for public docs?
Serve a public endpoint on Node

documents.text: Connect an MCP client to built documentation through four read-only tools. Use stdio for a client-launched local process, or enable an HTTP endpoint on Node or in a generated Vercel function. Both use the same search and Markdown reading core. The HTTP endpoint currently supports one explicitly selected public publication. The generated Vercel endpoint is deployed and verified on this site. Netlify and Cloudflare adapters are not implemented. Analytics is off by default; an optional server adapter can measure tool calls. You need Node.js 22.12 or newer, a built copy of Shoalrun, and a client that supports MCP stdio or Streamable HTTP. The compiler and CLI are still a private prototype; there is no public package to install yet. Why offer MCP for public docs? MCP gives tool-capable agents a predictable way to search your docs and request a page or section within a token budget. For example, an agent answering “How do I configure analytics?” can search and follow the returned read instruction. The result includes relevant Markdown, its publication, and a source link. The documentation can already be public. MCP adds a tool interface; it does not grant access that public Markdown lacks. Agents that can fetch and search your Markdown may not need it. Offer both when your readers use MCP clients, and check whether the tools help them find answers with fewer requests or less content. To use Shoalrun's own live documentation endpoint, follow use this site's MCP . The setup below is for hosting your own project's tools. Serve a public endpoint on Node Use this procedure when agents should connect to a URL instead of launching the CLI themselves. Analytics is not enabled by this setting. Enable a public publication Add the endpoint and the exact channel, version, and language to your project config. The selected publication must contain public pages: docs.config.yaml mcp : enabled : true access : public path : /mcp publication : { channel : production , version : current , language : en } The endpoint supplies those publication coordinates when the client omits them. Requests for a different publication are rejected. Its lexical search index is generated even if browser search is disabled. Build and serve the site With the CLI available as shoalrun , build the output and start the Node server: shoalrun build docs.config.yaml dist shoalrun serve dist --port 8774 The server reads the MCP settings from that build. It does not need the source config. With no site base path, the local endpoint is http://127.0.0.1:8774/mcp ; a base path such as /docs makes it /docs/mcp . Set mcp: false or remove the setting and rebuild to disable the endpoint. Restart a non-watching server after replacing its build; watched preview reloads settings with each successful build. Connect and check the tools Add the endpoint URL in your client’s remote MCP settings. The client should discover the four tools listed below. Search for a known page, then follow the returned read instruction and verify its publication. The SDK integration is tested with legacy and automatic protocol negotiation using MCP TypeScript client version 2.2.0 . Compatibility with a specific desktop client or public host still needs its own check. Hosts, origins, and limits Local connections permit the configured loopback host. For a public Node deployment, site.origin supplies a trusted hostname and browser origin. Add explicit mcp.allowedHosts hostnames for other domains and mcp.allowedOrigins origins for browser-based clients. Forwarded host headers are not trusted. Native clients do not need an Origin header. The endpoint accepts JSON MCP requests through POST; it does not provide a persistent session or standalone event stream. GET and DELETE return 405. Browser preflight uses OPTIONS. Limits are 64 KiB per request, eight concurrent requests per handler, and a 15-second deadline. Excess concurrent requests return 429 with retry guidance. Tool token budgets still apply. These are process-local controls; configure deployment-level limits before exposing a public service. This is a public endpoint, not an authentication mechanism for private documentation. Generate a Vercel endpoint With the public MCP configuration above, generate deployment output from your project: shoalrun vercel build docs.config.yaml .vercel/output No extra MCP flag, Ask configuration, embeddings, or model key is required. The command packages the four tools and their selected public documentation in a Node function at the configured endpoint. Internal runtime files stay out of the public static output. Follow Publish on Vercel to deploy the complete output directory. The function trusts site.origin , explicit allowed hosts, and Vercel’s reserved deployment host variables. It does not trust arbitrary forwarded hosts or other projects’ preview domains. Deployment protection may block an MCP client from reaching a preview; check that host setting if a client cannot connect. Returned Markdown links us

documents.title: Organize site navigation
documents.summary: Arrange guides, reference pages, and other documents into a clear site menu.

headings.title: Optionally split a large menu into files

documents.text: The navigation setting controls the site's left menu. It can be a list in docs.config.yaml or import a separate YAML file. Add guides, tutorials, concepts, and reference pages by their stable document IDs. Nodes appear in the order you write them. Each node has a stable id for the menu entry. It needs exactly one of these targets: doc places any page, including a guide or API reference, by its stable document ID. label with items makes a group of pages or nested groups. operation places an API reference by stable operation ID. generated fills in API references from the registered OpenAPI source. The menu follows document IDs rather than file paths or slugs. Moving a source file or changing a page URL does not require a navigation edit. A doc node uses the page title by default; set label when the menu needs a shorter name. Pages omitted from navigation can still be built and linked from other pages. Arrange authored pages - id : overview doc : guide.overview - id : learn label : Learn items : - id : first-steps doc : guide.first-steps label : First steps - id : core-concepts doc : concept.core - id : tasks label : Tasks items : - id : create-payment doc : guide.create-payment - id : handle-errors doc : guide.handle-errors Each doc value must match a page's frontmatter ID. Groups can contain other groups, so a larger site can place task guides under a product area. Use a structure that matches the reader's tasks; the source directory layout does not control the menu. The build rejects missing document IDs and malformed groups. For a publication where a page has no matching channel, version, or language, its menu entry is omitted. An empty group is omitted too. Use search on an individual page or operation node to add terms to the reader's sidebar menu filter . The filter also matches the page label and its group labels. For example, search: refunds returns helps readers find a page whose title uses different words. This setting does not add terms to the site-wide search index; site search uses page content and search metadata. Groups and generators cannot have search . Split navigation into tabs Use navigation tabs for parallel sections such as Guides, API reference, and Recipes. Mark a top-level group with tab: true and name its landing page by stable document ID: config/nav.yaml - id : guides label : Guides tab : true landing : guide.overview items : - { id : overview , doc : guide.overview } - { id : first-page , doc : guide.add-page } - id : api label : API reference tab : true landing : guide.api-references items : - { id : api-intro , doc : guide.api-references } - { id : generated , api : notes , generated : tags } Replace the example IDs and API name with your project's values. A tab ID uses lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens and starts with a letter. Tabs require a label, nonempty items, and a landing document inside those items. Nested tabs fail the build. A published page can belong to only one tab, or to shared navigation; placing it in both fails the build. Tabs whose items have no pages in a publication are omitted. A nonempty tab whose landing page is unavailable in that publication fails the build. Each tab links to its landing page. The current page's URL selects its tab and sidebar on the server. Opening a direct link, following a search result, or navigating without JavaScript selects the same section. Groups outside tabs remain shared navigation. A page outside every tab shows the shared navigation with no tab selected. Existing navigation lists work without adding tabs. Tab placement does not change page URLs or publication routes. The section links appear below the masthead on docs and wide pages. Landing and splash pages hide them by default. Set showNavigationTabs: true or false in page frontmatter to override the layout default; see page layouts . On smaller screens they use a Sections disclosure. They inherit each theme's typography and colors. Site-wide search still includes all sections; the sidebar filter searches only the current sidebar. Reader views can filter that sidebar without changing tab membership or agent discovery. Agent discovery across tabs Both /llms.min.txt and /llms.txt keep every published page and add links to a scoped text index for each tab and publication. Follow the published indexUrl ; do not construct it from the page's URL. Each scoped index links to all of that tab's Markdown pages and back to the global index, which also includes shared pages and pages omitted from navigation. Each member page's Markdown identifies its navigation section, stable tab ID, and scoped index. Its breadcrumbs include the tab. documents.json publishes a navigationTabs catalog and a matching navigationTab record on each member page. Records contain id , label , variant , url , markdownUrl , and indexUrl . Both search indexes carry page membership too. The generated offline documentation bundle includes the scoped indexes. Tab selection never removes page content from Markd

documents.title: Non-goals
documents.summary: Deliberate limits on Shoalrun's scope, including automatic skill builders, general agent orchestration, and using reader views for authorization.

headings.title: Shipping a skill builder with the tool

documents.text: Shoalrun's scope includes publishing documentation that people and agents can discover and read. This page records capabilities we deliberately exclude and the reasoning behind those decisions. Shipping a skill builder with the tool Shoalrun does not ship a non-interactive skill builder or automatically generate a reader-side skill for each site it builds. Skills need a human expert to guide their creation and maintenance. That expert brings knowledge of the domain, decides which workflows are appropriate, tests the instructions against real tasks, and keeps them accurate as the product changes. A non-interactive builder could produce something that looks complete and give users false confidence that they have “automatic agent skills.” Generating instructions alone does not establish that those instructions are useful, reliable, or kept current. We are not yet comfortable shipping a feature that implies that confidence. Shoalrun's bundled authoring skills are maintained instructions for working with Shoalrun. Published sites receive Markdown pages and discovery files during the build. Teams that create their own skills remain responsible for expert guidance, review, evaluation, and maintenance. General agent orchestration Shoalrun provides authoring tools for project discovery, documentation references, snapshot validation, and local review. The author's coding agent owns planning, evidence gathering, editing, its model, and execution permissions. General orchestration of arbitrary agents and tasks remains outside Shoalrun's scope. The evaluation task format and audit hook let teams use their own agents to run tasks and record reviewed results against a build. Shoalrun checks the report; the team owns agent execution and grading. Using reader views for authorization Reader views shape navigation and visible sections. They do not protect content: published files and Markdown twins remain available. Using a reader's selected view as an authorization boundary is outside their purpose. Exclude nonpublic pages from a public build and use host-level authorization when private content must be protected. Related reading Reference while working Bundled agent skills — See the maintained authoring skills that Shoalrun bundles. Related topics Evaluate agent tasks against your docs — Understand why agent execution remains outside Shoalrun. Agent-friendly documentation — See how published Markdown and discovery files help agents read a site. Bundled agent skills — Understand why a non-interactive skill builder is outside the tool's scope. Project status — Distinguish deliberate scope limits from deferred features.

documents.title: OpenAPI extension mappings
documents.summary: Map selected operation-level x-* values into Shoalrun metadata without depending on a particular authoring service.
documents.text: OpenAPI permits specification extensions whose names begin with x- . Their names and values belong to the tool or team that wrote the description. Shoalrun reads standard OpenAPI fields directly and applies an extension only when the project config explicitly maps it to a supported Shoalrun field. Supported mapping Use these source locations and value shapes when mapping OpenAPI extensions to Shoalrun fields. Shoalrun target Source location Accepted source shape Shoalrun values subjectLifecycle An operation under paths or OpenAPI 3.1 webhooks A scalar x-* value, or a scalar member inside an x-* object beta , in-development , experimental , deprecated Use apis.<apiId>.mappings.subjectLifecycle . from starts with an operation-level x-* key. For an object, add a dot and the member name; further simple member names may follow. values maps exact source values to Shoalrun values. Unlisted, missing, null, array, or object values do not set a badge. documents.title: OpenAPI support and limits
documents.summary: Check supported OpenAPI operations, schema keywords, examples, and source restrictions before importing a specification.

headings.title: Check a source before adding pages

documents.text: Shoalrun renders a defined subset of OpenAPI into HTML, Markdown, and focused contracts. Check these limits before importing a large specification. A supported OpenAPI version does not mean every feature in that version can be rendered. Compatibility The supported behavior varies by OpenAPI feature and source structure. Area Supported behavior Source formats OpenAPI 3.0.x and 3.1.x in YAML or JSON. kind: file builds from local files; api import can create a pinned local snapshot from a public HTTPS URL. Operations Method and path, server alternatives, CommonMark descriptions, security alternatives and credential details, path and operation parameter overrides, request body media types, responses, and named examples. Webhooks Top-level OpenAPI 3.1 webhooks , including a document without paths ; authored and generated references describe the inbound request and acknowledgement, with no outbound cURL command. Focused contracts retain the webhooks location. Authentication API keys in headers, query strings, or cookies; HTTP schemes; OAuth2 flow names and scopes; OpenID Connect discovery; mutual TLS. These describe authentication; the site does not authenticate or execute requests. References Local $ref within the project or configured OpenAPI source directory, including multiple files. api import downloads same-origin relative references and rewrites them to local snapshot paths. Recursive schemas end with a named reference marker. Absolute file paths and references escaping those directories are rejected. Schemas Objects, arrays, titled variants, discriminators, enums, constants, required fields, defaults, examples, nullable values, supported constraints, additional properties, and read/write/deprecated labels. OpenAPI 3.1 boolean schemas are supported. The exact keyword list is below. Named examples Parameter, request, and response examples maps; reusable components.examples references; names, summaries, descriptions, values, provenance, HTML selection and deep links. All examples appear in Markdown. HTTPS externalValue is an external link, not a fetched payload. Focused contracts One-operation JSON with transitive local components, named examples, security schemes, and internal recursive references. Enabled by source.focused: true or source.publish: true . Reader layout Three columns at wide widths and a stacked order on narrow screens. JSON schemas supply type shapes even without named examples; shapes and named examples are distinct views. Extension metadata Explicit mappings from operation-level x-* values to subjectLifecycle ; OpenAPI deprecated: true takes precedence. Other extensions do not automatically become page metadata. Supported schema keywords The renderer accepts these schema keys, plus x-* extension keys: $ref, type, format, nullable, enum, const, default, minLength, maxLength, minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, multipleOf, minItems, maxItems, uniqueItems, minProperties, maxProperties, pattern, readOnly, writeOnly, deprecated, description, example, examples, allOf, oneOf, anyOf, items, properties, required, additionalProperties, title, discriminator Other schema keywords fail when encountered by the renderer. This includes valid OpenAPI or JSON Schema keywords outside this list. The compiler presents supported constraints; it is not a general validator for payloads or the entire OpenAPI specification. Exclusive bounds follow the entry document's version even when a schema lives in another local file. In OpenAPI 3.0, exclusiveMinimum and exclusiveMaximum are booleans that modify a numeric minimum or maximum . In OpenAPI 3.1, each exclusive bound is a number. The build rejects a value in the wrong form. OpenAPI 3.1 also accepts true and false as entire schemas, displayed as allowing any value or no value, and an examples array on a schema. OpenAPI 3.0 rejects boolean schemas and schema-level examples . Features requiring adaptation These features have limits that may require adapting the source or authored documentation. Feature Current limit and recovery Remote $ref in a normal build Fails with Remote $ref requires a pinned snapshot . Use api import for public HTTPS sources with same-origin relative references, then build from its local snapshot. Cross-origin references need a separately prepared local source. Local externalValue Fails with local externalValue needs a pinned adapter . Use a local inline example value, or an HTTPS external example link. Callbacks Operation callbacks fail with an unsupported feature diagnostic. Top-level 3.1 webhooks are supported separately. Response headers and links Fail with Response headers or links need an adapter . Prepare a supported documentation source while retaining the original contract separately. Parameter content Requires an adapter; use supported parameter schemas in the documentation source. Request media encoding Fails with Request encoding needs an adapter . Multipart binary fields have limited generated upload commands, bu

documents.title: Publishing and agent representations
documents.summary: Read the published-output contract for HTML, Markdown, manifests, and incremental sync.
documents.text: shoalrun build turns accepted source pages and local OpenAPI files into a static site. A publication is one enabled channel, version, and language combination, such as production, v1, and English. The build includes a public page only in publications matching its frontmatter. It makes no model calls or remote requests. For each included page, the build writes an HTML page for browsing. It also writes a Markdown twin , a generated .md copy that agents can read as text. The Markdown twin can start with a short YAML header. That header contains only the page metadata selected in project config, so agents get useful context without a long source header or internal notes. Shared content appears in both bodies; authors can also add content to either format alone with Only . The site also includes a document manifest , documents.json , which indexes the built pages and their URLs. Projects with an API source can publish operation pages and focused contracts , small OpenAPI files containing one operation and the definitions it needs. Published-output contract This page is the consumer reference for Shoalrun's current published output. It describes the existing producer, not a general format that other generators must implement. The manifest and sync snapshot use schemaVersion: 1 . Editorial revisions to this reference do not change that wire version. The repository maintains JSON Schema 2020-12 definitions at framework/schemas/manifest.schema.json and framework/schemas/sync.schema.json . They specify required fields and known value shapes; this reference explains their meaning. Schema identifiers are stable names for local resolution, not a promise that a site hosts the schema files. Register both schemas together when validating a sync snapshot. They remain repository validation resources and are not added to site output. Consumers must tolerate unknown properties. Optional fields may be absent; absence is not evidence of a negative claim. Removing a required field, changing a field's meaning, or making existing valid output incompatible requires a new wire version. Adding optional fields can retain version 1. Changes to a constrained value set also need compatibility review; accepting unknown properties does not mean a consumer accepts unknown enum values. Capability Availability HTML and Markdown pages Every included public page has both representations. Manifest, sync snapshot, build information, response headers, redirect inventory, and both text discovery indexes Emitted by the build. Empty inventories are allowed. Search indexes Both full and compact indexes are emitted when search indexing is enabled. Section resources Emitted only for eligible sections of sufficiently long pages. Focused contracts and published API sources Emitted when configured for an API source. Sitemap Requires a site origin and enabled indexing. Markdown negotiation, redirect responses, caching, and HTTP 404 status Hosting behavior; the Node server and Vercel adapter implement it. Other hosts need matching rules. Routes include the configured base path and publication prefixes. Start at llms.min.txt under that base path, choose a page by its ID, title, and summary, then fetch its Markdown URL. Fetch the manifest when you need structured metadata. Discovery cost depends on the corpus and tokenizer; the budget measured for this site is not a guarantee for every site. A document's identity is (id, channel, version, language) , not its title, URL, or array position. The same ID in two publications identifies two records. That tuple must be unique in both the manifest and sync snapshot. Cite it with the resource URL; for sections, also retain section identity and parent/section digests. A manifest array pointer is a link into that snapshot, not a permanent document identifier. indexable describes indexing, not access. demo: false means unmarked, not a verified service. Missing or null subjectLifecycle does not mean stable. verified is an author's review date, not compiler or independent verification. updated records content freshness and can be a calendar date or a timestamp with a timezone. Reader filters control presentation, not authorization. Page formats Both formats come from the same parsed content. Supported components preserve their documented shared content in Markdown: tab choices, disclosure bodies, reader-marked branches, table rows, resolved snippets, and API examples retain readable content and relevant labels. Unknown components and unsupported dynamic MDX fail compilation. Explicit format-specific branches follow author selection; authors must review equivalent task guidance and completeness. Rendering checks do not prove semantic equivalence or that a reader has every prerequisite. Tabs become labeled sections in Markdown. OpenAPI examples and schemas are expanded during the build, so their values and field details appear as readable text in the twin. A filtered or sticky table keeps every row as a plain table in Markdown

documents.title: Color palettes
documents.summary: Use a built-in palette or extend one with your brand colors. The build checks every palette against WCAG contrast.
documents.text: A palette sets every color token on the site, with one set for light mode and one for dark mode. Choose a built-in palette by name, or extend one with your own colors. Built-in palettes Choose a built-in palette as the starting point for your site colors. Palette Colors kelp Sea green on white. The light set matches the base tokens in tokens.css . coral Coral accent over cool blue-gray neutrals. ink Black ink on warm paper with a vermilion accent. harbor Navy ink, blue links, and a yellow callout rule. amethyst Violet accents over lavender neutrals. vice Flamingo pink and aqua by day, and neon on a night-purple sky after dark. docs.config.yaml theme : palette : amethyst Each preset has a default palette, so you only need palette to change it. Add brand colors Extend a built-in palette and override only the tokens you need. Write token names without the --color- prefix: docs.config.yaml theme : palette : extends : harbor light : accent : "#0a6a48" link : "#0a6a48" emphasis : "#0a6a48" dark : accent : "#4fd6a4" accent-contrast : "#06231a" link : "#7fe0bd" extends defaults to the preset's palette. light and dark are both optional. Values must be three- or six-digit hex colors such as "#0a6a48" . Quote them, because YAML treats # as the start of a comment. To keep the colors in their own files, include each mode's token map and keep extends in the main config: docs.config.yaml theme : palette : extends : harbor light : { $include : ./styles/brand-light.yaml } dark : { $include : ./styles/brand-dark.yaml } styles/brand-light.yaml accent : "#0a6a48" link : "#0a6a48" Don't include a file that sets extends at its top level. The config loader reads a top-level extends in any config file as a list of config presets , so extends: harbor there fails the build. Most brands need four tokens or fewer: Token Controls accent Brand mark, primary header button, and active navigation marker. accent-contrast Text on accent , such as the primary button label. link and link-hover Links at rest and on hover. emphasis Eyebrows, card icons, and search highlights. The CSS and theme reference lists every token. Contrast checks The build checks each palette against WCAG 2.2 before it writes any files. It checks the light set, the dark set, or both, depending on the mode . If a pair fails, the build stops and names it: Theme colors fail WCAG 2.2 contrast: - light: link #9fe6cc on page #ffffff is 1.40:1; needs 4.5:1 Success criterion 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 for text against its background. Success criterion 1.4.11 requires 3:1 for focus rings, form field borders, and the accent fill against the page. The build checks these pairs: Body text, muted text, links, headings, navigation text, and summaries on the page, surface, and field backgrounds. Hovered links, callout text, and inline code on their backgrounds. Body text, links, and labels in each callout type: note, tip, important, warning, and caution. Body text, links, and labels on each custom callout tone from callouts.tones . Active navigation, subject lifecycle badges, and required and optional field badges. Code text and code labels on code blocks. accent-contrast on accent , and strong-text on strong-surface . focus , field-border , and accent against the page and surface. Every built-in palette passes in both modes. The framework tests check them on every change. Check colors in CI shoalrun config validate runs the same check without building the site. It prints the same messages and exits with status 1 when a pair fails, so a CI step can stop a change before it merges: shoalrun config validate docs.config.yaml On success, its JSON output includes "contrast": { "status": "ok", "palette": "kelp", "modes": ["light"] } . shoalrun audit also fails on a contrast problem, because it builds the site. The check covers palette colors only. Colors you set in project CSS , and syntax colors from a named Shiki theme, are not checked. Test those yourself. The default site code theme derives its syntax colors from the palette and replaces any that fall below 4.5:1 with plain code text. Related reading Read first Themes — Pick the preset that the palette colors. Related topics Light and dark mode — A palette has one color set for light mode and one for dark mode.

documents.text: A passage index splits built Markdown pages into smaller pieces for retrieval. Each passage keeps its page title, heading path, and source link. Chat and custom passage-search providers use it to find relevant parts of a page. The built-in search box uses the separate page-level search-index.json . You do not need a passage index for normal static-site search. Create the files after building the site: Command Adds Provider requests shoalrun index ai/chunks.json , the passage text and metadata. None. shoalrun index --embed Passage index plus embedding metadata and vectors. Sends embedding input to the configured provider. Indexing leaves published page content unchanged. The files sit beside the build output, and you must rebuild the index when that output changes. Build the index Build the site, then run shoalrun index on the output directory: shoalrun build docs.config.yaml site-dist shoalrun index site-dist The command prints a summary as JSON: { "status" : "ok" , "documents" : 77 , "chunks" : 725 , "output" : "/path/to/site-dist/ai/chunks.json" } The command reads three files from the build output: File Use documents.json The list of published pages, with each page's ID, URL, publication, and digest. Each page's .md twin The text to split. search-index.json The heading IDs that passage links use. Optional. It writes ai/chunks.json . Without --embed , it makes no network requests. Run it after each build. It replaces the previous file. Indexing also prepares readable paragraphs, code lines, and table rows for passage-search results. Search requests use that prepared data instead of parsing Markdown on first use. If serving search rejects an older index, rerun shoalrun index site-dist . Existing embeddings remain usable when the passage text and embedding settings are unchanged. Because it reads built output, the index holds only published pages in each publication. Drafts and pages outside enabled publications never appear. How the default chunker splits a page The default chunker follows structure. It doesn't cut text into fixed-length windows. Split at ## and ### headings. Text before the first ## heading forms an intro passage. Headings at #### and below stay inside their section's text. Keep blocks whole. A paragraph, list, table, or code block is never cut mid-block, except for large tables in step 4. Fill passages up to 2,000 characters. A section longer than that splits between blocks into a first passage and later parts. Split large tables between rows. Each part repeats the table's header rows, so every row keeps its column names. Keep large code blocks whole. A code block over the limit becomes one passage that exceeds it. Fenced code never starts a heading, so # comments inside a fence don't split a section. Merge short sections into their first subsection. A section under 200 characters with a subsection below it joins that subsection's first passage. A short section with no subsection stays a passage of its own. These limits are fixed. You can't configure the chunker or replace it yet. The number of passages changes as the documentation grows. Most passages are a few hundred characters long, and nearly all stay under 2,000. What a passage contains Each entry in chunks describes one passage: ai/chunks.json { "id" : "guide.configuration#understand-the-three-stages" , "docId" : "guide.configuration" , "title" : "Organize project configuration" , "type" : "how-to" , "variant" : "production|current|en" , "headingPath" : [ "Understand the three stages" ] , "url" : "/configuration#understand-the-three-stages" , "markdownUrl" : "/configuration.md" , "text" : "Configuration takes effect in three stages:\n\n1. **Resolve co…" , "digest" : "be259c2f4c0c896d1fe25ed496ac642f97391744675e06ee844f09372e47767a" , "search" : { "schemaVersion" : 1 , "paragraphs" : [ "Configuration takes effect in three stages: …" ] , "literalLines" : [] } } Field Value id The passage ID. See Passage IDs . docId , title , type The page's ID, title, and type. variant The page's channel, version, and language, joined by | . Passages from different publications never mix. headingPath The ## and ### headings above the passage, outermost first. Empty for an intro passage. url The page URL, plus # and the section's heading ID when one exists. markdownUrl The page's Markdown twin. readerFilters Optional. The page's reader marks, such as { "audience": ["maintainers"] } . It is present only when the page has marks. Retrieval uses it to answer for one audience. text The passage's Markdown, without its own heading. digest A SHA-256 hash of the passage's embedding input. search Prepared result content: schemaVersion: 1 , explanatory paragraphs , and code/table literalLines . Generated navigation lists are excluded from the paragraphs. The file also records schemaVersion and a sourceDigest that changes when any page's digest changes. Embedding input The heading path isn't part of text . Anything that scores or embeds a passage reads the page

documents.title: Generate and refresh answer cards
documents.summary: Generate and review common answers ahead of time, then serve confirmed cards without a new chat-model answer.
documents.text: An answer card stores a reviewed answer to a recurring question. Generate cards after local chat works, then review their text before serving them. Start in your documentation project root with the CLI available. A confirmed card avoids generating a new answer. Matching still calls the embedding provider and relevance scorer. Note: An answer card is not a page card. Page cards preview another page; see Cards and collections . Answer cards are stored answers. What you need A site indexed with --embed . See Passage index . A chat section with rerank: jev and a cards setting. See Retrieval and chat settings . A configured chat service and the provider keys used by shoalrun ask . Card generation can make new provider requests each time it runs. List the questions Write the questions in a YAML or JSON file. Each is a string, or a mapping with question and aliases . Aliases are other ways to ask the same thing. config/answers.yaml - question : how do I reset my password aliases : [ forgot my password , change my password ] - question : how do I export my data The file can live anywhere. You pass its path to the next command. Build the cards Card generation uses providers and can produce different wording on each run: index --embed sends new or changed passages to the embedding provider. answers calls the embedding provider and scorer, then the chat model for questions that pass the coverage gate. Fallback and escalation settings can add chat-model calls. Run the commands, then review the generated file before publishing: shoalrun index site-dist --embed shoalrun answers site-dist --questions config/answers.yaml Each question goes through the normal retrieval and answer checks. The command turns off card reuse and direct excerpts while generating cards, so an accepted card contains a freshly written answer. It also embeds each kept question and its aliases for later similarity matching. A question the docs do not cover may be declined before a chat-model call. The command writes ai/answers.json and reports kept and skipped questions. It skips a question when: The docs don't cover it. The answer was hedged. The answer cites nothing. A check flagged a sentence, some code, or a citation. A skipped question is a signal. Either the docs need a page for it, or the question is too broad for one answer. ai/answers.json is plain JSON. Each card holds its question, aliases, answer, sources, and the digest of every passage behind it. Read the answers before you ship them. The command writes the whole file each time, so to drop a card, remove its question from your list and run the command again. How a card is used With chat.cards set, a question that opens a conversation is checked against cards in two steps: The query embedding provider embeds the new question. Its vector is compared with each card's question vectors. A card at least threshold similar is shortlisted. The default is 0.75. The relevance scorer checks whether the card's stored answer really answers this question. The card is used only at confirm or higher. The default is 0.9. A confirmed card needs no new chat-model answer. Similarity alone can confuse related questions, such as turning notifications on versus turning them off. Scorer confirmation is a separate check against the stored answer. If no card is confirmed, the question follows the normal answer pipeline. A follow-up never uses a card. A card also belongs to one publication and reader view, and a question asked in another view never uses it. --no-cards on shoalrun ask turns cards off for one run. Keep cards current A card records the digest of each source passage. When a passage changes, the card stops being used without a warning. Run shoalrun answers after documentation changes to refresh the cards. If ai/answers.json is missing, or was made with a different embedding model, ask says so and carries on without cards. Find questions worth a card The question log shows what readers ask. Questions that were asked at least twice, that the model answered cleanly, and that no card covers make good candidates. shoalrun ask-log ask.jsonl --cards-out candidates.yaml --cards-out writes a new file and never replaces one. Review the list and move the questions you want into your questions file. Change the repeat count with --min-repeats . See Keep a record of questions for how to record the log. Where cards work Cards work in the terminal, the local panel, and the Vercel chat function. For Vercel, build with --chat , then run shoalrun answers against the function's private site directory before deployment. The function reads site/ai/answers.json from that directory. A plain shoalrun vercel build --chat embeds passages but does not generate cards. This repository's npm run docs:build-all performs both steps. See Publish on Vercel for the deployment workflow. Related reading Reference while working CLI reference — Look up the answers and ask-log commands and the --no-cards option. Retrieval and chat settings — L

documents.title: Share pages across documentation versions
documents.summary: Versioning one docs site without copying every page: share unchanged pages, vary sections, and publish changed pages separately.

headings.title: Keep an unchanged page in one file
Change just one part of a shared page
Give each API version its own contract

documents.text: Say you support v1 and v2. Your setup instructions are mostly the same, but v2 has a new credential and one extra guide. You can keep the common instructions in one source file , show the right credential in each version, and publish the extra guide only in v2. Shoalrun calls each channel, version, and language combination a publication . You choose which publications a build makes. A Git branch or tag chooses which revision of the repository to build ; it does not automatically create a docs version. For separate sites such as stable and next, see publish separate docs sites from Git . Choose which versions exist This config publishes two versions at /v1 and /v2 : docs.config.yaml (fragment) publications : defaults : { channel : production , version : v1 , language : en } channels : production : { pathPrefix : "" } versions : v1 : { pathPrefix : /v1 } v2 : { pathPrefix : /v2 } enabled : - { channel : production , version : v1 , language : en } - { channel : production , version : v2 , language : en } enabled sets the combinations the build may publish. It does not create pages or fill gaps in them. The paths come from the prefixes above plus each page's slug . Keep an unchanged page in one file List the versions that should receive the page in its frontmatter. This one file creates /v1/start and /v2/start : content/start.mdx --- id : guide.start title : Get started summary : Set up your first request. type : guide slug : /start publications : - { channel : production , version : v1 } - { channel : production , version : v2 } language : en access : { policy : public } --- Install the client and create a project. The publications list is explicit: add a version when the page should appear there, and omit it when the page should not. Only enabled combinations are built. Keep the same id and slug in every publication so links and the Version menu can find the corresponding page. A shared file cannot also set page-level channel or version . Change just one part of a shared page Put version-specific content inside <ForPublication> . The rest of the page stays shared: Create a project, then choose a credential. < ForPublication version = "v1" > Use a legacy key. </ ForPublication > < ForPublication version = "v2" > Use a scoped key. [ Set permissions ](doc:guide.permissions) </ ForPublication > You can select a channel , version , language , or a combination, such as <ForPublication channel="sandbox" version="v2"> . Omitted attributes match any value. The block needs at least one attribute and ordinary block content. A doc: link inside a block resolves in that publication, so a v2-only target can live in a v2-only block. If a whole page changes substantially, write separate source files with the same id and slug , each with its own channel and version . If a page exists only in v2, write only its v2 file. You do not need a blank v1 copy. The Version menu shows a matching page only where one was published. Source choice Result One file listing v1 and v2 The same page appears at both paths. One file listing v1 and v2, with <ForPublication> blocks Shared text appears in both; each version gets its own selected blocks. Two files with the same ID, one for each version Each version gets different page content. One file assigned only to v2 The page appears only in v2. Run shoalrun build docs.config.yaml dist and inspect dist/documents.json for the actual pages and routes. Links, navigation, search, and the Version menu use those published variants. A link to a page missing from the current publication fails the build instead of sending readers to another version. Give each API version its own contract When API behavior differs by version, bind an OpenAPI file to each publication in apis.<name>.publications . The top-level API source belongs to publications.defaults . A shared guide can refer to the same stable operation ID in both versions; each version resolves that operation against its own API source. The build fails if a page needs an API operation but that publication has no source. See API references for the config and example configs for full projects. What agents receive Each published page has a Markdown copy at its route plus .md , such as /v1/start.md and /v2/start.md . These are separate artifacts built from the same source file. Each copy includes only its own <ForPublication> sections, so an agent reading v1 instructions does not see v2-only text. documents.json , search-index.json , and the site's agent discovery files list the published variants and their Markdown URLs. A missing version of a page has no Markdown copy or search result. Published outputs lists those files. For channel and prefix rules, see the publication configuration reference . Add a language To add a language such as Japanese, add its combination to enabled , then write a translated file for each page with that language . The translated file reuses the page's id and slug , so it is another

documents.title: Deploy your documentation
documents.summary: Build your site, choose Vercel or Node hosting, and verify the deployed HTML and Markdown.
documents.text: After the quickstart , you have a source project and a compiled Shoalrun CLI. Use the commands below from my-docs/ , with SHOALRUN_CLI still pointing to the checkout's framework/dist/cli.js . Prepare a release Set site.origin in docs.config.yaml to your public HTTPS origin. Then audit the project and build it: node "$SHOALRUN_CLI" audit docs.config.yaml node "$SHOALRUN_CLI" build docs.config.yaml dist Review the generated HTML, Markdown, and dist/documents.json . A build replaces its output directory; keep source files outside dist/ . If it fails, use troubleshooting . Choose a host Choose a hosting route based on the artifacts and server features your site needs. Hosting route What to deploy Vercel A source checkout containing the framework and your project; Vercel builds .vercel/output/ . Node server The compiled site plus the built framework and its installed dependencies, as described below. Another host The compiled files plus routing and headers implementing the HTTP contract . For a site hosted at /docs , set site.basePath: /docs . The Node and Vercel adapters serve the prefixed routes directly. On a static host that mounts a directory at /docs , publish the build output's docs/ subtree as that directory's root. Static hosts still need a proxy or routing rules for Markdown content negotiation. Node hosting On a machine with Node and npm, obtain your committed checkout containing framework/ and my-docs/ . From that checkout root: npm ci --prefix framework npm --prefix framework run build node framework/dist/cli.js build my-docs/docs.config.yaml my-docs/dist node framework/dist/cli.js serve my-docs/dist --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 The last command runs the server in the foreground. Configure your host's process manager to run it from the checkout root and restart it after a release. Route your public HTTPS endpoint to port 8080 using the host's proxy or load balancer. Preserve request Accept headers and response headers through that proxy. The Node server handles HTML, negotiated Markdown, explicit .md URLs, and discovery resources. For a local check, use http://localhost:8080/install/ and http://localhost:8080/install.md from the minimal starter. Replace those paths with your own pages when you change the content. Other hosts A static upload alone does not establish Markdown content negotiation. Configure the host to serve the resources and page variants described in content negotiation , including Vary: Accept , content types, Markdown alternate links, redirects, and 404 responses. Use generated outputs to identify the files to deploy. Verify the public site From the checkout root, run the checker against your deployed origin: npm --prefix framework run deploy:check -- https://your-docs.example/ Check a deployed site explains the result and how to pass a URL with a base path. A local build verifies files; this check verifies the host's responses. Before sharing a page, check its SEO and social preview metadata , including the public share-image URL. Next, put multiple versions on one site if you need several editions in one site. For branches, tags, and retained build snapshots, see use Git branches for separate docs sites . Related reading Next steps Publish on Vercel — Build the site and routing rules for Vercel. Reference while working Check a deployed site — Check deployed HTML, Markdown, and discovery responses. Related topics Add Shoalrun to another build or host — Apply the hosting contract on another platform.

Then audit the project and build it: node "$SHOALRUN_CLI" audit docs.config.yaml node "$SHOALRUN_CLI" build docs.config.yaml dist Review the generated HTML, Markdown, and dist/documents.json . A build replaces its output directory; keep source files outside dist/ . If it fails, use troubleshooting . Choose a host Choose a hosting route based on the artifacts and server features your site needs. Hosting route What to deploy Vercel A source checkout containing the framework and your project; Vercel builds .vercel/output/ . Node server The compiled site plus the built framework and its installed dependencies, as described below. Another host The compiled files plus routing and headers implementing the HTTP contract . For a site hosted at /docs , set site.basePath: /docs . The Node and Vercel adapters serve the prefixed routes directly. On a static host that mounts a directory at /docs , publish the build output's docs/ subtree as that directory's root. Static hosts still need a proxy or routing rules for Markdown content negotiation. Node hosting On a machine with Node and npm, obtain your committed checkout containing framework/ and my-docs/ . From that checkout root: npm ci --prefix framework npm --prefix framework run build node framework/dist/cli.js build my-docs/docs.config.yaml my-docs/dist node framework/dist/cli.js serve my-docs/dist --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 The last command runs the server in the foreground. Configure your host's process manager to run it from the checkout root and restart it after a release. Route your public HTTPS endpoint to port 8080 using the host's proxy or load balancer. Preserve request Accept headers and response headers through that proxy. The Node server handles HTML, negotiated Markdown, explicit .md URLs, and discovery resources. For a local check, use http://localhost:8080/install/ and http://localhost:8080/install.md from the minimal starter. Replace those paths with your own pages when you change the content. Other hosts A static upload alone does not establish Markdown content negotiation. Configure the host to serve the resources and page variants described in content negotiation , including Vary: Accept , content types, Markdown alternate links, redirects, and 404 responses. Use generated outputs to identify the files to deploy. Verify the public site From the checkout root, run the checker against your deployed origin: npm --prefix framework run deploy:check -- https://your-docs.example/ Check a deployed site explains the result and how to pass a URL with a base path. A local build verifies files; this check verifies the host's responses. Before sharing a page, check its SEO and social preview metadata , including the public share-image URL. Next, put multiple versions on one site if you need several editions in one site. For branches, tags, and retained build snapshots, see use Git branches for separate docs sites . Related reading Next steps Reference while working Related topics

Publish on Vercel — Build the site and routing rules for Vercel. Check a deployed site — Check deployed HTML, Markdown, and discovery responses. Add Shoalrun to another build or host — Apply the hosting contract on another platform.

documents.text: A reader view changes which pages appear in navigation and search. It also controls document cards and marked sections within pages. The site still publishes one URL for each page. A first-time visitor sees all content; a choice is saved in the browser and added to the URL so it can be shared. Reader views are visibility controls, not access controls. All published page and section content remains available in site files and Markdown twins. Use access.policy to exclude a page from a public build, and host-level authorization to protect private content. Try the controls here Filter the navigation This site's Focus dropdown changes navigation, search, and document cards. The same control appears in the header on every page. Your choice persists across visits and can be shared in the URL. Choose Write documentation to bring forward pages about metadata, authoring, components, and API documentation. Pages about styling and deployment leave the navigation and search results. Choose Configure & publish to bring forward styling, search, chat, hosting, and deployment. Authoring-specific pages leave the navigation and search results. Choose All to see both paths. Foundational pages, such as How Shoalrun works , stay in every view. All published pages still work at their direct URLs. A focus choice is a reading aid, not an access rule. This site's focus facet has write and configure choices. Generated API references use a typeDefaults mark of write . It also retains an internal audience facet for the hosted chat's author view and a persona facet for the page-only examples below. The header shows only Focus. These machine IDs contain no spaces; the longer labels are only shown to readers. Filter examples on this page The controls below use a separate persona facet and scope="page" . They change the examples below without changing this site's navigation or search. Choose a reader to see one example, or use the controls to show both. Show UI example Show developer example UI example In a dashboard guide, show the menu names and screen actions a reader needs. This section appears when UI reader is selected. Developer example In an API guide, show the request, required fields, and expected response. This section appears when Developer is selected. Show all in the multi-select keeps both sections visible on this page. Follow site view removes the page-only choice and returns to the site's current reader view. The page-only choice is shareable with Copy view link and is not saved across visits. Configure the choices Define the available reader choices once in readerFilters.facets in docs.config.yaml . The facet names and choices are yours; Shoalrun has no fixed list of reader types. Each facet and choice has a stable lowercase ID and a label for readers. Pages and sections refer to these IDs, and unknown IDs fail the build. typeDefaults is optional; it is useful when generated API references should start in the Developer view without marking every operation separately. docs.config.yaml readerFilters : facets : audience : label : Reader options : ui : Use the UI developer : Build with the API product : label : Product options : payments : Payments reports : Reports area : label : Area options : reporting : Reporting setup : Setup subarea : label : Subarea options : settlements : Settlements exports : Exports typeDefaults : api-reference : audience : [ developer ] controls : sidebar : false header : { facet : audience , display : select , label : Reader } Nothing is selected by default, so every page and section is visible. Readers can select more than one choice within a facet: a page marked for either selected choice appears. Different facets combine: a page marked audience: [ui] and product: [payments] appears when both selections match. A page with no mark for a facet is shared across that facet. Mark pages Use the existing audiences field for the audience facet. product , area , and subarea can each supply a single choice for a same-named facet. Use readerFilters for other facets or when a page needs multiple choices in one facet. All of these fields work with frontmatter defaults and enforced values. content/payments-dashboard.mdx --- id : guide.payments-dashboard title : Review payments in the dashboard type : guide slug : /payments/dashboard audiences : [ ui ] product : payments area : reporting subarea : settlements --- When a facet is configured, audiences and same-named category values must use its choice IDs. You can instead use readerFilters.audience or readerFilters.product , but do not put both forms for the same facet on one page. An explicit page value overrides a typeDefaults value for that facet. Categories without matching configured facets remain taxonomy metadata only. Pages with no marks remain visible in every view. The page marks control navigation, search, and cards that point to the page. They do not change its URL. A direct link to a page outside the current view opens the page in full. A noti
